100 million for the Chief Credit Officer. Transactions exceeding these limits must be escalated to the next authority level, as
outlined in Section 3.
Aggregate exposure limits are applied to counterparties, industries, and geographic regions to prevent excessive concentration
risk. For example, the bank’s single counterparty exposure limit is set at 10% of its Tier 1 capital, while the aggregate exposure
to any single industry sector cannot exceed 20% of Tier 1 capital. Exposures approaching or exceeding 80% of these limits
must be escalated to the CCO for review, and any breaches must be reported to the Board of Directors within 48 hours. The
bank’s Risk Management Division (RMD) monitors aggregate exposures in real-time and generates automated alerts when
thresholds are approached.
In addition to exposure limits, the bank enforces risk-based thresholds for specific credit metrics. For corporate borrowers,
these include a maximum leverage ratio of 4.5x, a minimum interest coverage ratio of 2.0x, and a minimum current ratio of 1.2x.
For retail portfolios, thresholds include a maximum delinquency rate of 3% and a minimum FICO score of 650 for new
originations. Transactions or portfolios breaching these thresholds must be escalated according to the severity of the breach,
with more significant deviations requiring higher levels of approval.
The bank also applies concentration limits to specific asset classes and products. For example, exposures to commercial real
estate (CRE) cannot exceed 300% of the bank’s total risk-weighted assets, and within the CRE portfolio, no more than 15% of
the total CRE exposure can be concentrated in a single geographic market. Similarly, the bank limits its exposure to
speculative-grade (below BB-) counterparties to 5% of Tier 1 capital. Any transaction that would cause the bank to exceed
these concentration limits must be escalated to the CCO for exception approval.
Quantitative limits and thresholds are reviewed quarterly by the CPC, which may adjust them based on changes in the bank’s
risk appetite, capital position, or macroeconomic outlook. The CCO has the authority to impose temporary, more restrictive
limits in response to emerging risks or market dislocations. All changes to quantitative limits must be documented in the bank’s
policy management system and communicated to relevant stakeholders within 5 business days of approval.

Aggregate exposure limits are applied to counterparties, industries, and geographic regions to prevent excessive concentration
risk. For example, the bank’s single counterparty exposure limit is set at 10% of its Tier 1 capital, while the aggregate exposure
to any single industry sector cannot exceed 20% of Tier 1 capital. Exposures approaching or exceeding 80% of these limits
must be escalated to the CCO for review, and any breaches must be reported to the Board of Directors within 48 hours. The
bank’s Risk Management Division (RMD) monitors aggregate exposures in real-time and generates automated alerts when
thresholds are approached.
In addition to exposure limits, the bank enforces risk-based thresholds for specific credit metrics. For corporate borrowers,
these include a maximum leverage ratio of 4.5x, a minimum interest coverage ratio of 2.0x, and a minimum current ratio of 1.2x.
For retail portfolios, thresholds include a maximum delinquency rate of 3% and a minimum FICO score of 650 for new
originations. Transactions or portfolios breaching these thresholds must be escalated according to the severity of the breach,
with more significant deviations requiring higher levels of approval.
The bank also applies concentration limits to specific asset classes and products. For example, exposures to commercial real
estate (CRE) cannot exceed 300% of the bank’s total risk-weighted assets, and within the CRE portfolio, no more than 15% of
the total CRE exposure can be concentrated in a single geographic market. Similarly, the bank limits its exposure to
speculative-grade (below BB-) counterparties to 5% of Tier 1 capital. Any transaction that would cause the bank to exceed
these concentration limits must be escalated to the CCO for exception approval.
Quantitative limits and thresholds are reviewed quarterly by the CPC, which may adjust them based on changes in the bank’s
risk appetite, capital position, or macroeconomic outlook. The CCO has the authority to impose temporary, more restrictive
limits in response to emerging risks or market dislocations. All changes to quantitative limits must be documented in the bank’s
policy management system and communicated to relevant stakeholders within 5 business days of approval.

6. 6. Approval Workflows and Delegated Authority
Approval workflows under this policy are designed to ensure that credit decisions are made efficiently while maintaining robust
risk controls. The workflows are automated through the bank’s Credit Management System (CMS), which routes transactions to
the appropriate authority based on predefined rules, including transaction size, counterparty risk rating, and product type. The
CMS also flags transactions that require escalation due to policy exceptions, threshold breaches, or qualitative risk factors,
ensuring that no high-risk transaction is approved without the necessary oversight.
For transactions within a Relationship Manager’s (RM) delegated authority, the workflow requires the RM to complete a credit
application in the CMS, which includes a detailed assessment of the borrower’s creditworthiness, proposed terms, and
supporting documentation (e.g., financial statements, collateral valuations). The CMS automatically validates the application
against the bank’s underwriting criteria and quantitative thresholds. If the transaction complies with all requirements, the RM
may approve it directly. However, if the CMS identifies any issues, the transaction is automatically escalated to the BUCO for
review.
Transactions requiring BUCO approval follow a similar process, with the BUCO conducting an independent review of the RM’s
assessment. The BUCO must document their rationale for approval or rejection in the CMS, including any mitigating factors or
additional controls they deem necessary. If the BUCO approves the transaction, it is automatically routed to the RCO for
information purposes, though RCO approval is not required unless the transaction exceeds the BUCO’s delegated authority.
The CMS maintains a log of all approvals, including timestamps and the identities of the approving authorities, to ensure full
auditability.
For transactions requiring RCO or CCO approval, the workflow includes additional steps to ensure thorough due diligence. The
RCO or CCO must convene a credit review committee (CRC), which includes representatives from Risk Management, Legal,
Compliance, and the relevant business unit. The CRC reviews the transaction in detail, including a presentation by the RM and
a challenge session led by the RCO or CCO. The CRC’s recommendation is documented in the CMS, and the final decision is
recorded with the approving authority’s digital signature. Transactions requiring Board approval follow a similar process, with
the CCO presenting the case to the Board’s Risk Committee for ratification.
Delegated authority may be temporarily suspended or revised by the CCO in cases of repeated policy breaches, significant
credit losses, or changes in the risk profile of a business unit or region. The CCO must notify affected employees in writing and
update the CMS to reflect the changes. Delegated authority is also subject to annual recertification, which requires employees
to demonstrate ongoing competence in credit risk management through training and assessments. Failure to complete
recertification results in the automatic revocation of delegated authority until the requirements are met.

7. 7. Monitoring and Trigger Events
Monitoring is a critical component of the bank’s credit escalation framework, ensuring that risks are identified and addressed
proactively. The bank employs a multi-layered monitoring approach, combining automated surveillance tools with manual
reviews by credit and risk professionals. The primary objective is to detect early warning signals of credit deterioration, policy
breaches, or emerging risks that may require escalation under this policy.
The bank’s Credit Management System (CMS) includes a real-time monitoring module that tracks key credit metrics for all
counterparties, including financial ratios, risk ratings, covenant compliance, and exposure levels. The system generates
automated alerts when predefined thresholds are breached, such as a decline in a borrower’s risk rating, a breach of financial
covenants, or an increase in exposure beyond approved limits. These alerts are routed to the relevant Relationship Manager
and their supervisor, with escalation to higher authorities if the issue is not resolved within the stipulated timeframe.
In addition to automated monitoring, the bank conducts periodic manual reviews of credit portfolios to identify qualitative risks
that may not be captured by quantitative thresholds. For example, the Portfolio Risk Management team performs quarterly
reviews of high-risk industries, such as commercial real estate or leveraged lending, to assess the impact of macroeconomic
trends on credit quality. These reviews may trigger escalations to the RCO or CCO if they identify systemic risks or the need for
portfolio-level actions, such as increased provisions or reduced exposures.
Trigger events that mandate escalation under this policy include, but are not limited to, the following: a borrower’s risk rating
downgrade by two or more notches within a 12-month period; a breach of any financial or non-financial covenant that is not
cured within the grace period; a material adverse change in the borrower’s business, such as a significant loss of market share,
regulatory action, or litigation; or the identification of fraud, misrepresentation, or other integrity issues. The RM must escalate
such events to the BUCO within 24 hours of identification, with further escalation to the RCO or CCO as determined by the
severity of the issue.
The bank’s Internal Audit function conducts independent reviews of the monitoring and escalation processes at least annually.
These reviews assess the effectiveness of automated alerts, the timeliness of escalations, and the adequacy of actions taken to
address identified risks. Findings from these reviews are reported to the CCO and the Board’s Audit Committee, with corrective
actions tracked to completion. The CCO may also commission targeted reviews of specific portfolios or business units in
response to emerging risks or regulatory concerns.

8. 8. Exception Handling and Waivers
Exceptions to the bank’s standard credit policies, including underwriting criteria, quantitative thresholds, or approval workflows,
are permitted only under strictly controlled circumstances. This section outlines the process for requesting, reviewing, and
approving exceptions, as well as the controls in place to ensure that such exceptions do not expose the bank to unacceptable
risks. All exceptions must be justified by compelling business or strategic rationale and must be supported by robust risk
mitigants.
The process for requesting an exception begins with the Relationship Manager (RM), who must submit a formal exception
request through the Credit Management System (CMS). The request must include a detailed business case, an assessment of
the incremental risk introduced by the exception, and a description of the mitigating factors or controls that will be implemented
to offset the risk. The RM must also provide evidence that the borrower or transaction has been subjected to enhanced due
diligence, such as additional financial analysis, third-party risk assessments, or legal opinions.
Exception requests are reviewed by the Business Unit Credit Officer (BUCO), who assesses the merits of the case and the
adequacy of the proposed mitigants. The BUCO may approve exceptions for transactions within their delegated authority,
provided that the incremental risk is deemed acceptable and the mitigants are sufficient. However, exceptions that involve
policy breaches, such as waivers of standard covenants or underwriting criteria, must be escalated to the Regional Credit
Officer (RCO) for approval. The RCO may consult with the bank’s Risk Management Division (RMD) or Legal team to assess
the implications of the exception.
Exceptions that cannot be resolved at the RCO level, or those involving transactions exceeding USD 25 million, must be
escalated to the Chief Credit Officer (CCO). The CCO has the authority to approve exceptions that are consistent with the
bank’s risk appetite and strategic objectives. However, exceptions that involve material deviations from the bank’s credit
policies, such as transactions with counterparties rated below B- or exposures exceeding 15% of Tier 1 capital, require the
approval of the Board’s Risk Committee. The CCO must present such cases to the committee, including a detailed risk
assessment and a recommendation for approval or rejection.
All approved exceptions are documented in the CMS, with clear records of the rationale, the mitigating factors, and the identities
of the approving authorities. The bank’s Internal Audit function conducts periodic reviews of exception handling to ensure
compliance with this policy and to assess the effectiveness of the controls in place. Exceptions are also subject to post-approval
monitoring, with the RM required to provide quarterly updates on the performance of the transaction and the continued validity
of the mitigating factors. If the risk profile of the transaction deteriorates, the RM must escalate the case for reassessment,
which may result in the withdrawal of the exception or the imposition of additional controls.

9. 9. Reporting and Documentation Requirements
Comprehensive reporting and documentation are essential to the transparency, accountability, and auditability of the bank’s
credit escalation processes. This section establishes the requirements for documenting escalations, approvals, exceptions, and
monitoring activities, as well as the reporting obligations for various stakeholders, including senior management, the Board of
Directors, and regulatory authorities.
All escalations, approvals, and exceptions must be documented in the bank’s Credit Management System (CMS) at the time
they occur. The CMS captures key details, including the transaction size, counterparty information, risk ratings, underwriting
criteria, and the rationale for escalation or exception. The system also records the identities of the individuals involved in the
decision-making process, along with timestamps and digital signatures to ensure non-repudiation. Supporting documentation,
such as financial statements, risk assessments, and legal opinions, must be attached to the CMS record and retained for a
minimum of seven years.
The bank produces a series of standard reports to monitor compliance with this policy and to provide visibility into credit risk
exposures. These include daily reports of new escalations and approvals, which are distributed to the relevant Business Unit
Credit Officers (BUCOs) and Regional Credit Officers (RCOs). Weekly reports summarize the status of all open escalations,
including those awaiting approval, those under review, and those that have been rejected or withdrawn. Monthly reports provide
a more comprehensive view of escalation trends, including the volume and value of escalated transactions, the reasons for
escalation, and the average time taken to resolve escalations.
Quarterly, the bank prepares a Credit Escalation and Exception Report for the Chief Credit Officer (CCO) and the Credit Policy
Committee (CPC). This report includes an analysis of escalation patterns, such as the most common triggers for escalation, the
business units or regions with the highest escalation volumes, and the approval rates at each authority level. The report also
highlights any systemic issues or recurring policy breaches, along with recommendations for corrective actions or policy
updates. The CCO presents this report to the Board’s Risk Committee, which uses it to assess the effectiveness of the bank’s
credit risk management framework.
In addition to internal reporting, the bank is required to provide certain information to regulatory authorities as part of its ongoing
supervisory obligations. This includes regular reports on credit risk exposures, policy exceptions, and the bank’s adherence to
regulatory capital and liquidity requirements. The bank’s Regulatory Reporting team is responsible for compiling this
information, with input from the Credit Risk, Finance, and Compliance departments. All regulatory reports are reviewed by the
CCO and the Chief Financial Officer (CFO) prior to submission to ensure accuracy and completeness.
The bank’s Internal Audit function conducts periodic reviews of the reporting and documentation processes to ensure
compliance with this policy and to assess the adequacy of the controls in place. These reviews include testing the accuracy and
completeness of CMS records, the timeliness of reporting, and the effectiveness of the bank’s data governance framework.
Findings from these reviews are reported to the CCO and the Board’s Audit Committee, with corrective actions tracked to
completion.

10. 10. Policy Review and Continuous Improvement
This policy is subject to regular review to ensure that it remains aligned with the bank’s risk appetite, regulatory requirements,
and industry best practices. The review process is designed to identify opportunities for improvement, address emerging risks,
and incorporate lessons learned from the bank’s credit activities and external developments. The Chief Credit Officer (CCO) is
responsible for overseeing the review process, with input from the Credit Policy Committee (CPC), Risk Management Division
(RMD), and other relevant stakeholders.
The policy is reviewed at least annually, or more frequently if triggered by material changes in the bank’s operating
environment. Trigger events for an ad-hoc review include, but are not limited to, significant credit losses, regulatory changes,
mergers or acquisitions, or shifts in the bank’s strategic direction. The CCO may also initiate a review in response to findings
from internal audits, external examinations, or risk assessments that identify gaps or deficiencies in the escalation framework.
The review process begins with an assessment of the policy’s effectiveness, which is conducted by the CPC in collaboration
with the RMD. This assessment includes an analysis of escalation data from the Credit Management System (CMS), such as
the volume and value of escalated transactions, the reasons for escalation, and the outcomes of the escalation process. The
assessment also evaluates the timeliness of escalations, the adequacy of approval workflows, and the effectiveness of
monitoring and reporting mechanisms. Feedback is solicited from business units, risk professionals, and other stakeholders to
identify practical challenges or areas for improvement.
Based on the findings of the assessment, the CPC develops recommendations for updates to the policy. These
recommendations may include revisions to quantitative thresholds, underwriting criteria, or approval workflows, as well as
enhancements to the CMS or other supporting systems. The CPC presents its recommendations to the CCO, who reviews
them for alignment with the bank’s risk appetite and strategic objectives. If the CCO approves the recommendations, they are
formalized into a revised version of the policy and submitted to the Board’s Risk Committee for ratification.
Once approved, the revised policy is communicated to all relevant stakeholders through the bank’s policy management system,
with a clear implementation timeline and any required training or system updates. The CCO is responsible for ensuring that the
revised policy is effectively implemented and that all employees are aware of their obligations under the new framework. The
bank’s Internal Audit function may conduct a post-implementation review to verify compliance with the revised policy and to
assess its effectiveness in addressing the identified issues.
Continuous improvement is a core principle of the bank’s credit risk management framework. The CCO encourages a culture of
open communication and feedback, where employees at all levels are empowered to identify and report potential improvements
to the escalation process. The bank also benchmarks its policies and practices against industry peers and regulatory
expectations to ensure that it remains at the forefront of credit risk management. By fostering a proactive and adaptive
approach to policy review, the bank aims to maintain a robust and resilient credit escalation framework that supports its
long-term success.

1. 1. Purpose and Objectives
This synthetic credit policy document, designated as Clause A.1 under the parent policy REG-Basel-IV, establishes the
framework for Risk-Weighted Asset (RWA) treatment within the bank’s credit risk management operations. The primary
purpose of this policy is to ensure compliance with Basel IV standards while aligning internal credit risk assessments with
regulatory capital requirements. By defining clear methodologies for RWA calculation, this policy aims to enhance the accuracy
of capital adequacy reporting and support prudent risk-taking.
The objectives of this policy include: (i) providing a structured approach to assigning risk weights to credit exposures; (ii)
ensuring consistency in the application of RWA treatments across all business units; (iii) facilitating transparency in the bank’s
capital allocation processes; and (iv) enabling effective monitoring of credit risk concentrations. This policy is designed to be
internally consistent with the bank’s broader risk management framework, including credit underwriting, portfolio monitoring,
and regulatory reporting.
This document is synthetic demonstration data and does not reflect the actual policies, procedures, or practices of any real
financial institution. It is intended solely for illustrative purposes to demonstrate how a bank might structure its RWA treatment
policy under Basel IV. All thresholds, roles, and processes described herein are fictional and should not be interpreted as
operational guidelines.
The policy is grounded in the principle that RWA calculations must reflect the true economic risk of credit exposures. To achieve
this, the bank adopts a combination of the Standardized Approach and the Internal Ratings-Based (IRB) Approach, as
permitted under Basel IV. The choice of approach depends on the nature of the exposure, the availability of historical data, and
the sophistication of the bank’s risk management systems. The policy ensures that all approaches are applied consistently and
are subject to regular validation.
Compliance with this policy is mandatory for all business units involved in credit risk management, including lending, treasury,
and risk control functions. Failure to adhere to the RWA treatment guidelines may result in misalignment with regulatory capital
requirements, potentially leading to reputational, financial, or regulatory risks. The policy is reviewed annually to ensure its
continued relevance and alignment with evolving regulatory expectations.

responsibility for ensuring compliance with Basel IV and this policy. The Board delegates operational responsibility to the Group
Chief Risk Officer (CRO), who is accountable for the implementation, monitoring, and enforcement of the RWA treatment
methodologies. The CRO is supported by the Risk Management Committee (RMC), which provides strategic oversight and
approves any material changes to the policy.

developing and maintaining the methodologies, tools, and systems used for RWA calculations. The CRD is also tasked with
conducting periodic validations of the RWA models to ensure their accuracy and reliability. Any discrepancies or issues
identified during these validations must be escalated to the RMC for resolution.
Business units, such as Corporate Banking, Retail Banking, and Treasury, are responsible for ensuring that their credit
exposures are classified and reported in accordance with the RWA treatment policy. Each business unit must designate a

policy within their respective areas. These officers are required to undergo annual training on RWA treatment methodologies
and regulatory updates.

ensures that any identified deficiencies are addressed promptly.

4. 4. Underwriting Criteria and Risk Classification
The underwriting criteria for RWA treatment are aligned with the bank’s broader credit risk policies and are designed to ensure
that all exposures are classified accurately based on their risk characteristics. The policy mandates that all new credit
exposures undergo a comprehensive risk assessment before approval, which includes an evaluation of the borrower’s
creditworthiness, the nature of the exposure, and the availability of collateral or guarantees.
For corporate exposures, the bank uses a combination of external credit ratings and internal risk assessments to determine the
appropriate risk weight. Exposures to borrowers with an investment-grade rating (BBB- or higher) are assigned a risk weight of
50%, while those with a speculative-grade rating (BB+ or lower) are assigned a risk weight of 100% or higher, depending on the
specific rating. For unrated exposures, the bank applies its internal risk rating methodology, which categorizes borrowers into
risk buckets ranging from 1 (lowest risk) to 10 (highest risk), with corresponding risk weights of 20% to 150%.
Retail exposures, such as mortgages and personal loans, are subject to a separate risk classification framework. The bank
uses a scorecard-based approach to assess the creditworthiness of retail borrowers, with risk weights assigned based on the
probability of default (PD) and loss given default (LGD) estimates. For example, retail exposures with a PD of less than 1% are
assigned a risk weight of 35%, while those with a PD of 5% or higher are assigned a risk weight of 100%.
The policy also addresses the treatment of collateral and guarantees in RWA calculations. Collateralized exposures are eligible
for a reduction in risk weight, provided that the collateral meets the bank’s eligibility criteria and is legally enforceable. The
maximum reduction in risk weight is 50%, subject to a floor of 20%. Guarantees from eligible third parties, such as sovereigns
or highly rated financial institutions, may also result in a reduction in risk weight, depending on the credit quality of the
guarantor.

purposes. It includes fictional thresholds and methodologies to illustrate the complexity of aligning underwriting standards with
regulatory capital requirements. The criteria are designed to ensure that RWA calculations reflect the true risk of each exposure
while complying with Basel IV standards.

5. 5. Quantitative Limits and Thresholds
This policy establishes quantitative limits and thresholds to ensure that the bank’s RWA calculations remain within acceptable
risk parameters. The most critical threshold is the minimum capital requirement, which is set at 8% of total RWA, in line with
Basel IV. The bank’s internal target is to maintain a Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital ratio of at least 10%, providing a
buffer above the regulatory minimum to account for potential stress scenarios.
The policy also sets concentration limits for specific sectors, geographies, and borrower types to prevent excessive risk
exposure. For example, the bank limits its exposure to any single industry sector to 20% of total RWA. Similarly, exposures to
borrowers in high-risk jurisdictions, as defined by the bank’s country risk classification, are capped at 15% of total RWA. These
limits are monitored on a quarterly basis, and any breaches must be reported to the RMC within five business days.
In addition to concentration limits, the policy specifies thresholds for the use of internal models in RWA calculations. Under the
IRB Approach, the bank is permitted to use internal estimates of PD, LGD, and exposure at default (EAD) for certain asset
classes, provided that the models meet the regulatory criteria for validation and approval. The policy mandates that internal
models must be backtested annually, with a maximum tolerance of 5% deviation between estimated and actual outcomes.
Models that fail to meet this threshold are subject to remediation or replacement.
The bank also imposes limits on the use of credit risk mitigation techniques, such as collateral and guarantees. For example,
the policy states that the total reduction in RWA attributable to collateral and guarantees cannot exceed 30% of the bank’s total
RWA. This limit is designed to prevent over-reliance on risk mitigation techniques, which may not be effective in all scenarios.
The policy requires that all collateral and guarantees be revalued at least annually to ensure their continued eligibility for RWA
reduction.

calculations effectively. The thresholds and limits described herein are fictional and are intended to demonstrate the types of
constraints that a bank might impose to ensure compliance with Basel IV and internal risk management objectives.

6. 6. Approval Authorities and Escalation Paths
The approval authorities for RWA treatment are structured to ensure that decisions are made at the appropriate level of
seniority, based on the complexity and risk of the exposure. The policy defines three tiers of approval authority: (i) Business Unit
Heads, (ii) Regional Risk Committees, and (iii) the Group Risk Management Committee (RMC). Each tier has specific
delegated authorities and escalation paths to ensure that higher-risk decisions receive the necessary oversight.
Business Unit Heads are authorized to approve RWA treatments for exposures up to USD 10 million, provided that the
exposure complies with the bank’s standard underwriting criteria and risk classification frameworks. Approvals must be
documented in the bank’s credit approval system, with supporting evidence including the borrower’s credit rating, financial
statements, and collateral valuation (where applicable). Business Unit Heads are also responsible for ensuring that all approved
exposures are monitored in accordance with the policy’s monitoring requirements.
Regional Risk Committees (RRCs) are responsible for approving RWA treatments for exposures between USD 10 million and
USD 50 million, as well as any exposures that do not meet the standard underwriting criteria. The RRCs are composed of
senior representatives from the Credit Risk Department, Business Units, and Legal and Compliance functions. Approvals by the
RRCs must be supported by a detailed credit memo, which includes an analysis of the exposure’s risk characteristics, the
proposed RWA treatment, and any mitigating factors.
The Group RMC is the final approval authority for all exposures exceeding USD 50 million, as well as any exposures that
involve novel or complex structures, such as synthetic securitizations or credit derivatives. The RMC reviews these exposures
on a case-by-case basis, with input from the bank’s Legal, Compliance, and Finance departments. The RMC’s decision is
documented in a resolution, which is retained in the bank’s central repository for audit purposes.
Escalation paths are clearly defined to ensure that any disputes or exceptions to the policy are resolved promptly. For example,
if a Business Unit Head disagrees with the RWA treatment proposed by the Credit Risk Department, the matter must be
escalated to the relevant RRC for resolution. Similarly, if an RRC is unable to reach a consensus on a high-risk exposure, the
matter is escalated to the Group RMC. This synthetic escalation framework is designed to demonstrate how a bank might
ensure consistent and prudent decision-making in its RWA treatment processes.

The bank recognizes that there may be circumstances where strict adherence to the RWA treatment policy is not feasible or
appropriate. In such cases, the policy allows for exceptions and waivers, provided that they are justified, documented, and
approved in accordance with the bank’s governance framework. Exceptions and waivers are intended to provide flexibility while
maintaining prudent risk management practices.

of strategic importance to the bank. For example, an exception may be requested for a high-profile corporate client where the
bank has a long-standing relationship and a strong understanding of the client’s risk profile. Exceptions must be supported by a
detailed business case, which includes an analysis of the exposure’s risk characteristics, the proposed RWA treatment, and the
rationale for deviating from the policy.
Waivers may be granted for exposures where the application of the standard RWA treatment would result in an outcome that is
not aligned with the true economic risk of the exposure. For example, a waiver may be requested for a collateralized exposure
where the collateral’s value significantly exceeds the exposure amount, making the standard risk weight overly conservative.

proposed RWA treatment against alternative approaches.

The purpose of this Capital Floors Policy (the 'Policy') is to establish a robust framework for the implementation, monitoring, and
enforcement of capital floor requirements in accordance with the Basel IV regulatory standards. This Policy ensures that the
Bank maintains a minimum level of capital that mitigates risks arising from underestimation or miscalculation of risk-weighted
assets (RWAs) under internal models. By setting a floor, the Bank guarantees that its capital adequacy ratio does not fall below
a specified threshold, thereby safeguarding financial stability and regulatory compliance.
This Policy is designed to address the potential discrepancies between the Bank’s internal risk assessments and the
standardized approaches prescribed by regulatory authorities. It ensures that the Bank’s capital planning and risk management
practices are aligned with the principles of prudence, transparency, and accountability. The Policy also serves as a critical
control mechanism to prevent excessive leverage and to maintain public trust in the Bank’s financial resilience.
The Capital Floors Policy is a synthetic demonstration document created for illustrative purposes. It reflects industry best
practices and regulatory expectations but does not represent the actual policies, procedures, or practices of any real financial
institution. All thresholds, roles, and processes described herein are fictional and intended solely for training, testing, or
educational use.
This Policy applies universally across all business units, subsidiaries, and jurisdictions in which the Bank operates. It is binding
on all employees, contractors, and third parties acting on behalf of the Bank. Compliance with this Policy is mandatory, and any
deviations must be justified, documented, and approved through the established governance framework.
The Policy is reviewed annually or more frequently if there are significant changes in regulatory requirements, the Bank’s risk
profile, or its operational environment. The review process ensures that the Policy remains relevant, effective, and aligned with
the Bank’s strategic objectives and regulatory obligations.

2. 2. Scope
This Policy applies to all material risk exposures of the Bank, including but not limited to credit risk, market risk, operational risk,
and counterparty credit risk. It covers all business lines, legal entities, and geographical regions where the Bank conducts its
operations. The scope includes all internal models used for calculating RWAs, as well as the standardized approaches for
comparison and validation purposes.
The Capital Floors Policy is particularly relevant to the Bank’s Internal Ratings-Based (IRB) approaches for credit risk,
Advanced Measurement Approaches (AMA) for operational risk, and internal models for market risk. For each of these areas,
the Policy establishes a floor based on a percentage of the RWAs calculated using the standardized approach. The floor is set
at 72.5% of the standardized RWAs, as per Basel IV requirements, to ensure consistency and comparability.
Exposures that are not material in terms of their contribution to the Bank’s overall risk profile may be excluded from the scope of
this Policy, provided that such exclusions are justified, documented, and approved by the Risk Management Committee (RMC).
The materiality threshold for exclusion is defined as any exposure that constitutes less than 1% of the Bank’s total RWAs.
Exclusions must be reviewed annually to ensure they remain appropriate.
The Policy also applies to all new products, services, and business activities introduced by the Bank. Prior to launch, these
must undergo a capital floor assessment to ensure compliance with the Policy’s requirements. The assessment must be
conducted by the Risk Management Department (RMD) in collaboration with the relevant business unit and submitted to the
RMC for approval.
For jurisdictions where local regulations impose additional or different capital floor requirements, the Bank will comply with the
stricter of the two standards. The RMD is responsible for monitoring regulatory developments and ensuring that the Policy is
updated to reflect any changes in local or international requirements.

The underwriting criteria outlined in this section are designed to ensure that all credit exposures subject to the Capital Floors
Policy are originated and managed in a manner consistent with the Bank’s risk appetite and regulatory requirements. These
criteria apply to all new and renewed exposures, including loans, derivatives, and other credit facilities.

approval. The escalation must include a detailed analysis of the reasons for the breach, the potential risks, and the proposed

5. 5. Quantitative Limits
The Capital Floors Policy establishes quantitative limits to ensure that the Bank’s capital adequacy ratio remains above the
minimum regulatory requirements. The primary limit is the capital floor, which is set at 72.5% of the RWAs calculated using the
standardized approach. This means that the RWAs calculated under the Bank’s internal models must not be less than 72.5% of
the RWAs calculated under the standardized approach for the same exposures.
In addition to the capital floor, the Policy introduces a series of internal triggers and thresholds to monitor and manage capital
adequacy. The first trigger is activated when the Bank’s Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital ratio falls below 10.5%. At this
point, the RMD must conduct a detailed review of the Bank’s capital position and submit a report to the RMC within 10 business
days, outlining the causes of the decline and the proposed corrective actions.
A second trigger is activated when the CET1 capital ratio falls below 9.5%. In this case, the RMC must convene an emergency
meeting within 5 business days to assess the situation and develop a capital restoration plan. The plan must include specific

5. 5. Quantitative Limits
The Capital Floors Policy establishes quantitative limits to ensure that the Bank’s capital adequacy ratio remains above the
minimum regulatory requirements. The primary limit is the capital floor, which is set at 72.5% of the RWAs calculated using the
standardized approach. This means that the RWAs calculated under the Bank’s internal models must not be less than 72.5% of
the RWAs calculated under the standardized approach for the same exposures.
In addition to the capital floor, the Policy introduces a series of internal triggers and thresholds to monitor and manage capital
adequacy. The first trigger is activated when the Bank’s Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital ratio falls below 10.5%. At this
point, the RMD must conduct a detailed review of the Bank’s capital position and submit a report to the RMC within 10 business
days, outlining the causes of the decline and the proposed corrective actions.
A second trigger is activated when the CET1 capital ratio falls below 9.5%. In this case, the RMC must convene an emergency
meeting within 5 business days to assess the situation and develop a capital restoration plan. The plan must include specific
measures to improve the capital ratio, such as reducing risk-weighted assets, raising additional capital, or divesting non-core
assets. The plan must be approved by the Board and submitted to the relevant regulators within 15 business days.
The Policy also establishes a maximum leverage ratio of 5%, calculated as the ratio of the Bank’s Tier 1 capital to its total
exposure measure. The total exposure measure includes both on-balance sheet and off-balance sheet exposures. If the
leverage ratio exceeds 5%, the Bank must immediately notify the RMC and implement measures to reduce the ratio to within
the limit.

exceed 3 times the average VaR capital charge over the previous 60 business days. If this limit is breached, the Bank must

6. 6. Approvals
The approvals process under this Policy is designed to ensure that all material decisions related to capital floors are subject to
appropriate oversight and accountability. Approvals are required for the initial implementation of the Policy, any subsequent
amendments, and all exceptions or breaches of the Policy’s requirements.
Amendments to the Policy must be approved by the RMC and the Board. The process begins with a proposal from the RMD,
which is reviewed by the RMC. If the RMC approves the proposal, it is submitted to the Board for final approval. Amendments
are typically reviewed annually, but ad-hoc reviews may be conducted if there are significant changes in regulatory
requirements or the Bank’s risk profile.
Exceptions to the Policy’s requirements, such as exclusions from the scope or justifications for capital floor breaches, must be
approved by the RMC. Requests for exceptions must be submitted by the relevant business unit to the RMD, which conducts an
initial review and provides a recommendation to the RMC. The RMC considers the request at its next scheduled meeting or, if
urgent, at an ad-hoc meeting. Approvals for exceptions are valid for a maximum of 12 months, after which they must be
reviewed and reapproved.
Breaches of the capital floor or other quantitative limits must be reported to the RMC within 24 hours of identification. The RMC
must then determine whether the breach is material and, if so, escalate it to the Board. Material breaches are those that exceed
5% of the Bank’s total RWAs or result in a CET1 capital ratio below 9.5%. The RMC or Board, as applicable, must approve a
remediation plan to address the breach within 10 business days.
The Policy also requires approvals for the introduction of new internal models or significant changes to existing models. These
must be approved by the MVT, the RMC, and, in some cases, the relevant regulators. The approval process includes a
thorough validation of the model’s assumptions, methodologies, and performance, as well as an assessment of its impact on
the Bank’s capital floors.

8. 8. Exceptions
The Policy recognizes that there may be circumstances where strict adherence to the capital floor requirements is not feasible
or appropriate. In such cases, exceptions may be granted, provided that they are justified, documented, and approved through
the established governance framework. Exceptions are intended to be rare and are subject to strict controls and monitoring.
Exceptions may be requested for individual exposures, portfolios, or business units. Common reasons for exceptions include
the unavailability of reliable data for the standardized approach, the unique risk characteristics of an exposure that are not
captured by the internal models, or the temporary nature of a breach due to market conditions. However, exceptions cannot be
granted for systemic or persistent breaches of the capital floor.
Requests for exceptions must be submitted to the RMD using the standardized Exception Request Form. The form requires a
detailed justification for the exception, including the specific circumstances that warrant it, the potential risks, and the proposed
mitigation measures. The request must also include an assessment of the impact of the exception on the Bank’s capital
adequacy and a plan for monitoring and reviewing the exception.
The RMD reviews the request and provides a recommendation to the RMC. The RMC considers the request at its next
scheduled meeting or, if urgent, at an ad-hoc meeting. The RMC’s decision is based on the merits of the request, the potential
risks to the Bank, and the adequacy of the proposed mitigation measures. If approved, the exception is documented in the
Exception Register, which is maintained by the RMD and reviewed by the RMC on a quarterly basis.
Exceptions are valid for a maximum of 12 months, after which they must be reviewed and reapproved. The RMD is responsible
for monitoring the status of all exceptions and ensuring that they remain justified and appropriate. If the circumstances that
warranted the exception change, the RMD must reassess the exception and, if necessary, recommend its revocation to the
RMC.
All exceptions must be reported to the relevant regulators as part of the Bank’s regular regulatory reporting. The report must
include the number of exceptions, their justification, and the status of any remediation plans. The Bank must also be prepared
to provide additional information or explanations to the regulators upon request.

report provides an overview of the Bank’s overall capital floor compliance, including aggregate RWAs, capital floor ratios, and

implementation.

compliance. These reports are typically submitted quarterly and include detailed information on the Bank’s RWAs, capital floor
ratios, and any breaches or exceptions. The reports must be accurate, complete, and submitted by the regulatory deadlines.
The Policy also requires ad-hoc reporting for material breaches or exceptions. These reports must be submitted to the RMC
and the relevant regulators within 24 hours of identification. Ad-hoc reports must include a detailed description of the breach or
exception, its causes, the potential risks, and the proposed remediation plan. The RMC and regulators may request additional
information or explanations as needed.

Bank’s strategic objectives and regulatory requirements. Reviews are conducted at regular intervals and in response to
significant changes in the Bank’s operating environment or risk profile.

assessment of the Policy’s effectiveness in achieving its objectives, as well as an evaluation of its alignment with the Basel IV
requirements and other relevant regulations. The review also considers feedback from business units, the IAD, and the MVT, as

considers the results of the stress tests and scenario analyses conducted during the year.

by the RMD and submitted to the RMC for approval.

1. 1. Purpose and Applicability
This document, titled RAT-1.0 Credit Rating Standards, establishes the foundational framework for credit rating assignments
within the synthetic demonstration environment of the bank. It is designed to ensure consistency, transparency, and regulatory
compliance in the evaluation of creditworthiness for all counterparties, including corporate, commercial, and retail clients. The
standards outlined herein are aligned with the parent policy RAT-v1.0 and serve as a critical component of the bank’s risk
management infrastructure.
The primary purpose of RAT-1.0 is to define the methodologies, criteria, and governance structures required to assign, validate,
and monitor credit ratings. These ratings are integral to the bank’s decision-making processes, including loan approvals,
risk-based pricing, capital allocation, and portfolio monitoring. By adhering to these standards, the bank aims to mitigate credit
risk, enhance stakeholder confidence, and fulfill its fiduciary responsibilities.
This policy applies to all business units, risk management teams, and personnel involved in the credit assessment process. It is
mandatory for underwriters, credit analysts, relationship managers, and senior management to comply with the provisions of
this document. Third-party vendors or partners engaged in credit-related activities on behalf of the bank must also adhere to
these standards unless explicitly exempted by the Chief Risk Officer (CRO).
The synthetic nature of this document is emphasized to clarify that it is intended for demonstration, training, and internal testing
purposes only. While the thresholds, roles, and processes described are realistic and internally consistent, they do not reflect
actual bank operations or real-world data. Any use of this document for live transactions or external reporting must be explicitly
authorized by the bank’s compliance and legal departments.
The applicability of RAT-1.0 extends to all credit exposures, including but not limited to loans, bonds, derivatives, and trade
finance instruments. It covers both new credit applications and the periodic review of existing exposures. The standards are
designed to be scalable, accommodating the diverse needs of the bank’s global operations while maintaining uniformity in risk
assessment practices.

2. 2. Scope and Exclusions
The scope of RAT-1.0 Credit Rating Standards encompasses all credit rating activities conducted by the bank, including the
initial assignment, periodic review, and ad-hoc reassessment of ratings. This includes ratings for internal risk management
purposes as well as those used for regulatory reporting, such as under the Basel III framework. The policy is global in nature,
applying to all jurisdictions in which the bank operates, unless local regulations impose stricter requirements.
All credit exposures, regardless of size or complexity, fall within the scope of this policy. This includes exposures to corporate
entities, small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), retail customers, financial institutions, and sovereign entities. The policy
also covers specialized lending areas such as project finance, leveraged finance, and structured credit products. Each
exposure must be assigned a credit rating in accordance with the methodologies outlined in this document.
Exclusions from this policy are limited and must be explicitly documented and approved by the CRO. Typical exclusions may
include intra-group exposures, where the counterparty is a subsidiary or affiliate of the bank, and exposures that are fully
guaranteed by a sovereign entity with a risk weight of 0% under regulatory capital rules. Additionally, exposures that are
immaterial in size (defined as less than USD 100,000) may be exempted from formal rating assignments, provided they are
subject to alternative risk controls.
The policy also excludes credit ratings assigned by external credit rating agencies (e.g., Moody’s, S&P, Fitch) for the purpose of
regulatory compliance, where such ratings are used directly without internal override. However, the bank reserves the right to
perform its own internal rating assessment for risk management purposes, even when external ratings are available. In such
cases, the internal rating must be documented and justified in accordance with the standards set forth in this policy.
Any deviations from the scope of this policy, including temporary or permanent exclusions, must be documented in the bank’s
Risk Policy Exception Log. Such deviations require the approval of the CRO and must be reviewed at least annually to ensure
they remain appropriate. The bank’s internal audit function will periodically verify compliance with the scope and exclusion
provisions of this policy.

3. 3. Governance and Roles
The governance framework for RAT-1.0 Credit Rating Standards is designed to ensure accountability, independence, and
oversight in the credit rating process. The Board of Directors retains ultimate responsibility for the approval and periodic review
of this policy, delegating its implementation to the CRO. The CRO, in turn, is responsible for ensuring that the policy is applied
consistently across the bank and that all personnel adhere to its provisions.
The Credit Risk Management (CRM) department is the primary owner of this policy and is tasked with its day-to-day
administration. The CRM department is responsible for developing and maintaining the credit rating methodologies, tools, and
systems used by the bank. It also oversees the training of personnel involved in the rating process and ensures that all ratings
are assigned in accordance with the established criteria. The Head of CRM reports directly to the CRO and provides regular
updates on the performance and effectiveness of the rating standards.
Credit analysts and underwriters are responsible for the execution of the rating process, including the collection and analysis of
relevant data, the application of rating methodologies, and the documentation of rating rationales. These individuals must
possess the necessary qualifications and experience, as defined in the bank’s Competency Framework for Credit
Professionals. Analysts and underwriters are required to complete annual training on the RAT-1.0 standards and any updates
thereto.
The Independent Risk Validation (IRV) team plays a critical role in the governance framework by providing an independent
review of the credit rating process. The IRV team is responsible for validating the accuracy and consistency of ratings,
assessing the effectiveness of the rating methodologies, and identifying any potential biases or weaknesses in the process. The
IRV team reports its findings directly to the CRO and the Board’s Risk Committee, ensuring that any issues are addressed
promptly and transparently.
Escalation paths are clearly defined to resolve disputes or uncertainties in the rating process. If a credit analyst or underwriter

5. 5. Underwriting Criteria and Evidence Requirements
The underwriting criteria specified in RAT-1.0 are designed to ensure that credit decisions are based on a thorough and
rigorous analysis of all relevant factors. Underwriters must adhere to these criteria when evaluating new credit applications or
reviewing existing exposures. The criteria are structured to align with the bank’s risk appetite and regulatory expectations,
ensuring that only counterparties meeting the minimum standards are approved for credit facilities.
For corporate and commercial lending, underwriters are required to obtain and analyze a comprehensive set of financial
statements, including audited annual reports, interim financial statements, and management accounts. The financial statements
must cover at least the past three years, unless the counterparty is a startup or has a shorter operating history. Underwriters
must also review the counterparty’s business plan, cash flow projections, and any available market research reports.
In addition to financial data, underwriters must gather qualitative evidence to support their assessment. This includes
conducting site visits, interviewing key management personnel, and reviewing industry reports from reputable sources. For
counterparties operating in high-risk industries or jurisdictions, underwriters must also obtain independent third-party
assessments, such as due diligence reports or environmental, social, and governance (ESG) evaluations.
For retail lending, underwriters must verify the applicant’s identity, income, and employment status using primary sources, such
as government-issued identification, pay stubs, and employer verification letters. Credit reports from at least one major credit
bureau must be obtained and reviewed for all retail applicants. In cases where the applicant’s credit history is limited or
unavailable, underwriters may use alternative data sources, such as utility payment records or rental history, provided these are
documented and justified.
All evidence gathered during the underwriting process must be retained in the bank’s credit file system for a minimum of seven
years from the date of the last action on the credit facility. The evidence must be organized and labeled clearly to facilitate
future reviews or audits. Underwriters are responsible for ensuring that the credit file is complete and accurate before submitting
their recommendation to the appropriate approval authority.

6. 6. Quantitative Limits and Thresholds
RAT-1.0 establishes quantitative limits and thresholds to ensure that credit exposures are managed within the bank’s risk
appetite and regulatory constraints. These limits are designed to prevent excessive concentration of risk and to ensure that the
bank maintains adequate capital and liquidity buffers. The thresholds are applied at various levels, including individual
counterparties, industry sectors, geographic regions, and the overall portfolio.
For individual counterparties, the bank sets exposure limits based on the assigned credit rating. The maximum exposure to a
single counterparty is capped at 25% of the bank’s Tier 1 capital for investment-grade counterparties (rated BBB- or higher) and
10% of Tier 1 capital for sub-investment-grade counterparties (rated BB+ or lower). Exposures to retail counterparties are
subject to aggregate limits, with no single retail exposure exceeding 1% of Tier 1 capital.
Industry sector limits are established to prevent over-concentration in any single sector. The bank’s exposure to any one
industry sector may not exceed 20% of its total credit exposures. Sectors are defined using the Global Industry Classification
Standard (GICS), and exposures are aggregated at the two-digit GICS level. Geographic limits are also applied, with no single
country (excluding the bank’s home country) accounting for more than 15% of total credit exposures.
The bank also imposes internal risk-based limits, which are more granular than the regulatory limits. These include limits on the
proportion of the portfolio that can be assigned to each rating grade. For example, the bank targets that no more than 10% of its
total credit exposures should be rated BB+ or lower. Additionally, the bank sets thresholds for watchlist and non-performing
exposures, with the latter not exceeding 3% of total exposures at any time.
Quantitative limits are monitored on a daily basis by the bank’s Risk Monitoring team, which reports any breaches to the CRM
department and the relevant business units. Breaches must be addressed within 30 days, either by reducing the exposure or
obtaining a waiver from the CRO. All waivers must be documented and justified, with a clear action plan for remediation. The
bank’s internal audit function conducts quarterly reviews of limit compliance and breach management processes.

8. 8. Monitoring and Trigger Events
The monitoring framework specified in RAT-1.0 is designed to ensure that credit exposures are continuously assessed for
changes in risk profile, and that appropriate actions are taken in response to adverse developments. The bank employs a
combination of automated surveillance tools and manual reviews to monitor its credit portfolio, with the frequency and intensity
of monitoring proportional to the risk rating of the exposure.
All credit exposures are subject to automated monitoring on a daily basis, with the bank’s Risk Monitoring team tracking key
financial and non-financial indicators for signs of deterioration. These indicators include financial ratio trends, payment behavior,
credit rating changes, and adverse news events. Automated alerts are generated when predefined thresholds are breached,
such as a decline in the counterparty’s interest coverage ratio below 1.5x or a downgrade in its external credit rating.
In addition to automated monitoring, the bank conducts periodic manual reviews of its credit exposures. Investment-grade
exposures (rated BBB- or higher) are reviewed at least annually, while sub-investment-grade exposures (rated BB+ or lower)
are reviewed at least quarterly. Retail exposures are subject to ongoing behavioral monitoring, with individual accounts flagged
for review if they exhibit delinquency, over-limit usage, or other signs of stress.
Trigger events are defined as specific occurrences that necessitate an immediate review of the credit exposure. These include,
but are not limited to, a breach of financial covenants, a payment default, a material adverse change in the counterparty’s
financial condition, or a significant negative news event (e.g., regulatory action, litigation, or a natural disaster affecting the
counterparty’s operations). Upon the occurrence of a trigger event, the responsible relationship manager must initiate a review
within 5 business days and submit a recommendation to the appropriate approval authority within 10 business days.
The results of monitoring activities and trigger event reviews are documented in the bank’s Credit Monitoring System, with all
actions and rationales recorded for audit purposes. The Risk Monitoring team provides monthly reports to the CRM department
and the CRO, summarizing the number and nature of alerts, the outcomes of reviews, and any emerging trends or concerns.
The internal audit function conducts semi-annual reviews of the monitoring framework to assess its effectiveness and identify
any gaps or weaknesses.

9. 9. Exception Handling and Waivers
RAT-1.0 recognizes that there may be circumstances where strict adherence to the credit policy is not feasible or appropriate.
In such cases, the bank permits exceptions and waivers, provided they are properly justified, documented, and approved in
accordance with the framework outlined in this section. The exception handling process is designed to balance the need for
flexibility with the bank’s commitment to risk discipline and regulatory compliance.
An exception is defined as a deviation from the standard underwriting criteria, quantitative limits, or approval authorities
specified in this policy. Common examples of exceptions include approving a credit exposure that exceeds the counterparty’s
assigned limit, extending credit to a counterparty that does not meet the minimum financial thresholds, or delegating approval
authority beyond the permitted scope. Exceptions may also arise in cases where the counterparty’s risk profile is mitigated by
factors not fully captured by the standard criteria, such as strong collateral or third-party guarantees.
The process for requesting an exception begins with the submission of an Exception Request Form by the relationship manager
or underwriter. The form must include a detailed rationale for the exception, an assessment of the incremental risk, and a
description of any mitigating factors or controls. The request is then reviewed by the CRM department, which assesses its
compliance with the bank’s risk appetite and regulatory expectations. If the CRM department supports the request, it is
forwarded to the appropriate approval authority, which varies based on the nature and size of the exception.
Waivers are a subset of exceptions that involve temporary or permanent deviations from the policy’s quantitative limits or
thresholds. Waivers are typically granted in cases where the bank has a strategic or commercial rationale for accepting the
additional risk, such as supporting a long-standing client through a temporary period of financial stress. Waivers must be
approved by the CRO or the Global Credit Committee, depending on the size and risk profile of the exposure. All waivers are
subject to a maximum term of 12 months and must be reviewed at least quarterly to ensure they remain appropriate.
All exceptions and waivers are recorded in the bank’s Risk Policy Exception Log, which is maintained by the CRM department
and reviewed monthly by the CRO. The log includes details such as the nature of the exception, the rationale, the approval
authority, the date of approval, and the expiration date (if applicable). The internal audit function conducts annual reviews of the
exception handling process to ensure compliance with the policy and to identify any systemic issues or trends. Any exceptions
or waivers that result in a loss or near-miss event are subject to a post-mortem analysis, with findings reported to the Board’s
Risk Committee.

10. 10. Reporting and Review
The reporting and review requirements specified in RAT-1.0 are designed to ensure transparency, accountability, and
continuous improvement in the bank’s credit rating processes. The policy establishes a comprehensive framework for internal
and external reporting, as well as periodic reviews of the policy’s effectiveness and relevance.
Internal reporting is conducted at multiple levels, with the frequency and detail of reports tailored to the needs of the audience.
The Risk Monitoring team provides daily dashboards to the CRM department, summarizing key portfolio metrics such as
exposure concentrations, rating migrations, and limit breaches. Weekly reports are provided to the business units, highlighting
new approvals, monitoring alerts, and exception requests. Monthly reports are submitted to the CRO and the Global Credit
Committee, with a focus on emerging risks, trend analyses, and the status of remediation actions.
External reporting is conducted in accordance with regulatory requirements, such as those specified under the Basel III
framework and local banking regulations. The bank’s regulatory reports include detailed information on its credit portfolio, such
as exposure by rating grade, industry sector, and geographic region, as well as data on non-performing loans, past-due
exposures, and loan loss provisions. The CRM department is responsible for ensuring the accuracy and timeliness of all
external reports, which are subject to independent validation by the IRV team prior to submission.
The RAT-1.0 policy itself is subject to periodic review to ensure it remains aligned with the bank’s risk appetite, regulatory
expectations, and industry best practices. The policy is reviewed at least annually by the CRM department, with input from the
IRV team, internal audit, and the business units. The review process includes an assessment of the policy’s effectiveness in
mitigating credit risk, as well as an evaluation of any gaps or weaknesses identified through monitoring, audits, or loss events.
Material changes to the policy, such as updates to the credit rating methodologies, underwriting criteria, or quantitative limits,
require the approval of the CRO and the Board’s Risk Committee. The CRM department is responsible for communicating any
changes to the relevant stakeholders and ensuring that all personnel are trained on the updated provisions. The policy review
process is documented in the bank’s Policy Review Log, which includes details such as the date of the review, the key findings,
and the actions taken.

major loss, a regulatory change, or a shift in the bank’s strategic direction. The results of all reviews are reported to the Board of
Directors, with recommendations for any necessary updates or enhancements to the policy. The bank’s internal audit function
conducts an independent review of the policy at least once every three years, with findings and recommendations reported
directly to the Board’s Audit Committee.

robust covenant structures. Exposure to Tier 4 industries is subject to strict concentration limits, as outlined in Section 6.

must be consulted for exposures to Tier 3 and Tier 4 industries, and their input must be reflected in the credit memorandum.

decision-making.

6. 6. Quantitative Limits and Concentration Thresholds
The IND-1.0 Policy establishes quantitative limits to control industry concentration risk and ensure portfolio diversification.
These limits are designed to prevent excessive exposure to any single industry or group of related industries, thereby mitigating
the potential for significant losses due to industry-specific downturns.
The policy defines concentration limits at two levels: (1) Individual Industry Limits, which cap exposure to a single industry as a
percentage of the bank’s total credit portfolio; and (2) Industry Group Limits, which cap exposure to a group of related
industries. Individual Industry Limits are set at 5% for Tier 1 industries, 3% for Tier 2 industries, 2% for Tier 3 industries, and 1%
for Tier 4 industries.
Industry Group Limits are set at 15% for groups comprising Tier 1 and Tier 2 industries, 10% for groups including Tier 3
industries, and 5% for groups including Tier 4 industries. These limits are applied at the consolidated bank level and are
monitored on a monthly basis by the Industry Risk Team.
Breaches of concentration limits must be escalated to the CRC within five business days of identification. The CRC will evaluate
the breach and determine whether corrective action, such as risk mitigation or portfolio rebalancing, is required. Exceptions to
concentration limits require CRC approval and must be justified by compelling strategic or risk-adjusted return considerations.
This synthetic framework for quantitative limits is intended to demonstrate how concentration risk is managed within a credit
portfolio. The specific thresholds and escalation paths described are fictional and should not be applied in a real-world context
without customization.

7. 7. Approval Authorities and Delegation
The IND-1.0 Policy defines clear approval authorities and delegation limits to ensure that credit decisions are made at the
appropriate level of seniority, commensurate with the risk involved. Approval authorities are structured to align with the industry
risk tier and the size of the exposure.
For Tier 1 industries, credit officers with delegation limits up to $10 million may approve exposures without additional escalation,
provided all underwriting criteria are met. Exposures between $10 million and $50 million require approval from a Senior Credit
Officer, while exposures exceeding $50 million require CRC approval.
For Tier 2 industries, credit officers may approve exposures up to $5 million. Exposures between $5 million and $25 million
require Senior Credit Officer approval, and those exceeding $25 million require CRC approval. All exposures to Tier 3 industries
require Senior Credit Officer approval for amounts up to $10 million, with CRC approval required for larger exposures.
Exposures to Tier 4 industries require CRC approval regardless of size. Additionally, all new exposures to Tier 4 industries must
be accompanied by a detailed industry risk assessment and a risk mitigation plan, both of which must be approved by the CRC.
Delegation limits are reviewed annually by the CRC and adjusted as necessary to reflect changes in risk appetite or market
conditions.
This synthetic approval framework is designed to illustrate how authority and accountability are structured within a credit risk
management system. The delegation limits and approval paths described are fictional and intended for demonstration purposes
only.

8. 8. Monitoring and Early Warning Indicators
The IND-1.0 Policy mandates continuous monitoring of industry risk exposures to identify emerging risks and ensure
compliance with concentration limits. The Industry Risk Team is responsible for developing and maintaining a dashboard of key
industry risk metrics, which are reviewed monthly by the CRC.
Early Warning Indicators (EWIs) are used to detect potential deterioration in industry risk profiles. EWIs include financial metrics
such as declining profitability, increasing leverage, or deteriorating liquidity within an industry. Non-financial EWIs may include
regulatory changes, technological disruptions, or shifts in consumer demand.
The Industry Risk Team conducts quarterly deep-dive reviews of industries exhibiting EWI breaches or approaching
concentration limits. These reviews include an assessment of the root causes of the EWI breaches, the potential impact on the
bank’s portfolio, and recommended actions to mitigate risk. Findings are presented to the CRC for discussion and approval.
In addition to internal monitoring, the bank subscribes to external industry risk reports and macroeconomic analyses to
supplement its assessments. The Industry Risk Team integrates these external insights into its monitoring framework and
escalates material findings to the CRC as needed.
This synthetic monitoring framework is intended to demonstrate how industry risk is tracked and managed on an ongoing basis.
The EWIs, review processes, and escalation paths described are fictional and designed for illustrative purposes.

9. 9. Exception Management and Escalation
The IND-1.0 Policy establishes a formal exception management process to address instances where credit exposures deviate
from industry risk guidelines. Exceptions may arise due to strategic opportunities, client relationship considerations, or other
justifiable reasons, but they must be carefully evaluated and approved to ensure that risk is appropriately managed.
All exceptions to industry risk guidelines, including concentration limit breaches, underwriting criteria waivers, or approval
authority overrides, must be documented in the Exception Log. The log captures the nature of the exception, the rationale for
the deviation, the risk mitigation measures in place, and the approval authority. The Exception Log is maintained by the Industry
Risk Team and reviewed quarterly by the CRC.
Exceptions to concentration limits or underwriting criteria for Tier 3 and Tier 4 industries require CRC approval. For Tier 1 and
Tier 2 industries, exceptions may be approved by the Head of Credit Risk or a Senior Credit Officer, depending on the
materiality of the deviation. All exceptions must include a risk-adjusted return analysis to justify the deviation from policy.
Escalation paths are clearly defined to ensure timely resolution of exceptions. Credit officers or BUROs must escalate potential
exceptions to the Industry Risk Team within two business days of identification. The Industry Risk Team then evaluates the
exception and presents it to the appropriate approval authority. Urgent exceptions, such as those posing immediate risk to the
portfolio, must be escalated to the CRO within 24 hours.
This synthetic exception management process is designed to illustrate how deviations from policy are handled in a structured
and controlled manner. The escalation paths, approval authorities, and documentation requirements described are fictional and
intended for demonstration purposes.

assessing, mitigating, and monitoring credit risks arising from transactions denominated in foreign currencies. This policy

2. 2. Scope
The Foreign Currency Credit Risk Policy (CUR-1.0) applies to all business units, subsidiaries, and branches of the bank that
engage in transactions denominated in foreign currencies. This includes but is not limited to corporate lending, trade finance,
project finance, syndicated loans, and derivative transactions where the bank assumes credit risk in a currency other than its
functional currency. The policy covers both on-balance-sheet assets (e.g., loans, bonds) and off-balance-sheet exposures (e.g.,
guarantees, letters of credit, derivatives).
The scope of this policy extends to all counterparties, including corporate clients, financial institutions, sovereign entities, and
multilateral organizations. It applies regardless of the counterparty’s domicile or the jurisdiction in which the transaction is
booked. The policy is particularly relevant for transactions involving currencies that are not freely convertible or are subject to
exchange controls, as these introduce additional layers of risk that must be carefully managed.
Excluded from the scope of this policy are transactions denominated in the bank’s functional currency, as these are governed
by the bank’s domestic credit risk policies. Additionally, foreign exchange (FX) risk arising from non-credit transactions (e.g., FX
trading for proprietary purposes) is managed under the bank’s Market Risk Policy and is not addressed here. However, the
policy acknowledges the interplay between credit risk and FX risk and requires that both be considered holistically where
applicable.
The policy is binding on all employees, contractors, and third-party service providers acting on behalf of the bank in the
origination, execution, or management of foreign currency-denominated credit exposures. Compliance with this policy is
mandatory, and any deviations must be approved through the formal exception process outlined in Section 9. The policy is
synthetic demonstration data and is not intended to reflect the actual scope of any real financial institution’s operations.
The bank reserves the right to expand or contract the scope of this policy as its business activities evolve. Any material changes
to the scope will be communicated to all relevant stakeholders and will require approval from the bank’s Risk Policy Committee
(RPC). The policy is designed to be flexible enough to accommodate new products, markets, or counterparty types while
maintaining a consistent and rigorous approach to foreign currency credit risk management.
