9. 9. Reporting and Transparency
The bank maintains a comprehensive reporting framework to ensure transparency and accountability in the application of the
Spread Grid. The CRM department generates a monthly Spread Grid Compliance Report, which is distributed to the CPC,
business unit heads, and Internal Audit. The report includes metrics such as the number of transactions priced within the grid,
the frequency and magnitude of adjustments, the number of exceptions, and the average spread by risk bucket and business
unit.
The monthly report also highlights any control failures, such as transactions lacking required approvals or documentation, and
tracks the resolution of these issues. Business units are required to provide explanations for any material deviations from the
grid and to outline corrective actions. The CPC reviews the report to identify systemic issues or trends that may require policy
updates or additional training.
Quarterly, the CRM department produces a Spread Grid Performance Report, which analyzes the financial impact of the grid on
the bank’s portfolio. This report includes an assessment of the spreads’ effectiveness in compensating for credit losses, the
contribution of spreads to net interest margins, and the sensitivity of the portfolio to changes in market conditions. The report is
presented to the Board Risk Committee and used to inform strategic decisions, such as risk appetite adjustments or capital
allocation.
Annually, the bank publishes a summary of its Spread Grid framework in its Pillars 1 and 3 disclosures under Basel III. The
disclosure includes the methodology for determining spreads, the range of spreads applied to different risk buckets, and the
governance processes for approvals and exceptions. This transparency is intended to provide regulators, investors, and other
stakeholders with confidence in the bank’s risk management practices.
Ad hoc reporting is triggered by significant events, such as a breach of the bank’s risk appetite statement, a material change in
market conditions, or a regulatory inquiry. In such cases, the CRM department works with the affected business units to
produce a detailed analysis of the event’s impact on the Spread Grid and the broader credit portfolio. The findings are reported
to the CPC and, where necessary, to the Board of Directors.

10. 10. Policy Review and Maintenance
The Spread Grid is subject to periodic review to ensure that it remains relevant, effective, and aligned with the bank’s risk
appetite and regulatory expectations. The CRM department conducts a comprehensive review of the grid at least annually, with
input from business units, risk analytics, compliance, and Internal Audit. The review assesses the grid’s performance in
predicting credit losses, its consistency with market practices, and its compliance with regulatory requirements.
The annual review includes a validation of the quantitative inputs and thresholds used in the grid. The CRM department tests
the grid’s calibration by comparing actual default rates and loss severities to the predicted PD and LGD values. If the grid is
found to be miscalibrated (e.g., actual losses exceed expected losses for a given risk bucket), the thresholds or inputs are
adjusted accordingly. The review also considers feedback from underwriters and business units on the practicality and usability
of the grid.
Ad hoc reviews are conducted in response to material changes in the bank’s operating environment. For example, a significant
economic downturn, a new regulatory capital framework, or a merger or acquisition may necessitate an interim review of the
grid. The CPC has the authority to mandate such reviews and to fast-track updates to the grid if warranted. All ad hoc reviews
must be completed within 90 days of the triggering event.
Updates to the Spread Grid are approved by the CPC and communicated to all stakeholders through formal policy memos,
training sessions, and updates to the bank’s policy management system. The CRM department is responsible for ensuring that
all business units and risk functions are aware of the changes and have the necessary tools and training to implement them.
The effective date of updates is typically 30 days after approval, allowing time for systems updates and staff training.
The bank maintains a version control system for the Spread Grid, with each update assigned a unique version number and
effective date. The system tracks all changes, including the rationale for updates, the stakeholders consulted, and the approvals
obtained. This ensures transparency and accountability in the policy maintenance process. The current version of the Spread
Grid, as demonstrated in this synthetic document, is PRC-v1.7, Clause 1.2, effective as of the date of this policy.

4. 4. Underwriting Criteria
The underwriting criteria outlined in this synthetic policy are designed to ensure that all CRE loans adhere to the bank’s risk
appetite and sub-sector limits. Underwriters must evaluate each loan application against a set of qualitative and quantitative
criteria, which include but are not limited to borrower creditworthiness, property cash flow, loan-to-value (LTV) ratios, debt
service coverage ratios (DSCR), and sub-sector exposure.
For borrower creditworthiness, underwriters must assess the financial strength, experience, and track record of the borrower or
sponsoring entity. This includes a review of financial statements, credit history, and prior project performance. Borrowers must
demonstrate the ability to service debt obligations under stress scenarios, with a minimum DSCR of 1.25x for most sub-sectors.
Higher DSCR thresholds may be required for higher-risk sub-sectors, such as hospitality, where a minimum of 1.40x may apply.
Property-level underwriting must include a thorough analysis of the property’s cash flow, occupancy rates, tenant quality, and
market position. For office and retail properties, underwriters must evaluate lease rollover risk, tenant concentration, and the
property’s ability to attract and retain tenants. Industrial properties require an assessment of location, accessibility, and demand
drivers, while multifamily properties must demonstrate stable occupancy and rental income.
LTV ratios are capped at 70% for most sub-sectors, with stricter limits of 60% for higher-risk sub-sectors such as hospitality or
specialized real estate. Exceptions to these limits require approval from the CRE Risk Management Team and must be justified
by compensating factors, such as strong borrower credit or exceptional property cash flow.
Underwriters are also responsible for ensuring that the loan complies with the sub-sector exposure limits defined in Section 5. If
a loan approval would cause the bank’s exposure to a sub-sector to exceed its limit, the underwriter must escalate the request
to the CRE Risk Management Team for further review and potential exception processing.

5. 5. Quantitative Limits
This synthetic policy establishes quantitative limits for CRE sub-sector exposures to mitigate concentration risk and ensure
portfolio diversification. The limits are expressed as a percentage of the bank’s total CRE portfolio and are designed to prevent
over-exposure to any single sub-sector. The following thresholds apply: Office: 25%, Retail: 20%, Industrial: 20%, Multifamily:
25%, Hospitality: 10%, and Specialized Real Estate: 10%.
Sub-sector exposure is calculated as the aggregate outstanding loan balance for all loans secured by properties within a given
sub-sector, divided by the total outstanding balance of the CRE portfolio. The CRE Risk Management Team is responsible for
monitoring these exposures on a monthly basis and reporting any breaches or potential breaches to the Credit Risk Committee.
In addition to sub-sector limits, the policy imposes concentration limits for individual loans within a sub-sector. No single loan
may exceed 10% of the bank’s total CRE portfolio, and no single borrower or related group of borrowers may account for more
than 15% of the total CRE portfolio. These limits are designed to prevent excessive exposure to any single asset or borrower.
The policy also includes a buffer zone for sub-sector limits. If exposure to a sub-sector reaches 90% of its limit, the CRE Risk
Management Team must notify the Credit Risk Committee and implement a watchlist for that sub-sector. New loans in a
sub-sector on the watchlist require additional scrutiny and approval from the CCO or their delegate.
Quantitative limits are reviewed annually by the CRE Risk Management Team and may be adjusted based on changes in
market conditions, regulatory requirements, or the bank’s risk appetite. Any proposed changes to the limits must be approved
by the Credit Risk Committee and documented in a policy amendment.
For the purposes of this synthetic policy, all quantitative thresholds are hypothetical and designed to illustrate how a bank might
structure its CRE sub-sector limits. Actual limits in a real-world scenario would be tailored to the bank’s specific risk profile and

8. 8. Exceptions

underwriting criteria are justified. However, exceptions are granted only under strict conditions and with appropriate oversight to

An exception may be requested when a loan opportunity presents significant strategic value to the bank, such as a high-profile
client relationship, a unique market opportunity, or a transaction that aligns with the bank’s long-term goals. Exceptions may
also be considered for loans that demonstrate compensating factors, such as exceptionally strong borrower credit, superior
property cash flow, or robust collateral coverage.
The exception process begins with the submission of a formal request by the originating loan officer or underwriter to the CRE
Risk Management Team. The request must include a detailed justification for the exception, an analysis of the loan’s risk profile,
and an assessment of the impact on the bank’s sub-sector exposure. The CRE Risk Management Team reviews the request
and may consult with other stakeholders, such as the Regional Credit Officer or the Chief Credit Officer, as needed.
If the exception is approved, it must be documented in the bank’s exception log, which is maintained by the CRE Risk
Management Team. The log includes the date of approval, the names and titles of the approving authorities, the terms of the
exception, and any conditions or mitigating actions required. Exceptions are also reported to the Credit Risk Committee on a
quarterly basis for ongoing oversight.
Exceptions are subject to a sunset clause, meaning they are valid only for a specified period, typically not exceeding 12 months.
At the end of this period, the loan must either be brought into compliance with the policy or re-approved as an exception. The
CRE Risk Management Team is responsible for tracking exception expirations and ensuring timely renewals or corrections.

1. 1. Purpose and Applicability
This document, titled '2.2 Construction Guidance,' is a synthetic demonstration policy derived from the parent policy
SEC-CRE-v2.0. It establishes the framework for evaluating, approving, and managing credit exposures related to construction
financing within the bank. The purpose of this policy is to ensure that construction lending activities are conducted in a manner
consistent with the bank’s risk appetite, regulatory requirements, and industry best practices. This policy applies to all business
units, employees, and third parties involved in the origination, underwriting, administration, and monitoring of construction loans.
Construction lending presents unique risks, including cost overruns, delays, and market volatility, which require specialized
underwriting and monitoring. This policy provides clear guidelines to mitigate these risks while supporting the bank’s strategic
objectives in the construction sector. It is designed to align with the bank’s broader credit risk management framework, ensuring
consistency in decision-making and risk assessment across all construction-related credit exposures.
The policy is applicable to all construction loan types, including but not limited to commercial real estate development,
residential subdivision financing, and infrastructure projects. It covers both direct lending and participations in syndicated
construction facilities. Exclusions include permanent financing arrangements, which are governed by separate policies under
SEC-CRE-v2.0.
This document is synthetic and intended for demonstration purposes only. It does not reflect the actual policies, procedures, or
practices of any real financial institution. All thresholds, roles, and requirements outlined herein are fictional and designed to
illustrate a comprehensive credit policy framework for construction lending.
Compliance with this policy is mandatory for all employees involved in construction lending activities. Failure to adhere to the
guidelines set forth in this document may result in disciplinary action, up to and including termination of employment.
Additionally, non-compliance may expose the bank to heightened regulatory scrutiny, financial losses, or reputational damage.

2. 2. Scope and Definitions
The scope of this policy encompasses all construction loan activities, from initial application through final disbursement and
conversion to permanent financing or repayment. It applies globally across all jurisdictions where the bank operates, unless
superseded by local regulatory requirements. The policy governs the actions of relationship managers, credit analysts,
underwriters, risk managers, and senior leadership involved in the construction lending process.
For the purposes of this policy, 'construction lending' is defined as any financing arrangement where the primary use of
proceeds is the development, expansion, or rehabilitation of real estate assets. This includes both speculative and pre-sold
projects, as well as phased developments. The policy distinguishes between 'hard costs' (e.g., labor, materials) and 'soft costs'
(e.g., permits, architectural fees), both of which are subject to specific underwriting and disbursement controls.
Key definitions include: (1) 'Loan-to-Cost (LTC) Ratio': The ratio of the loan amount to the total estimated project cost,
expressed as a percentage. (2) 'Loan-to-Value (LTV) Ratio': The ratio of the loan amount to the appraised value of the
completed project. (3) 'Stabilized Occupancy': The occupancy rate at which a project is expected to generate sufficient cash
flow to cover debt service. (4) 'Contingency Reserve': A designated portion of the loan proceeds held back to cover unexpected
cost overruns.
The policy also defines roles and responsibilities, including the 'Relationship Manager,' who serves as the primary point of
contact for the borrower; the 'Credit Underwriter,' responsible for assessing the creditworthiness of the borrower and the viability
of the project; and the 'Construction Risk Officer,' who oversees compliance with this policy and reports to the Chief Credit
Officer.
All terms used in this policy are consistent with the bank’s internal glossary and regulatory definitions. Where conflicts arise, the
most conservative interpretation shall prevail. This section ensures that all stakeholders have a shared understanding of the
terminology and concepts critical to construction lending.

3. 3. Governance and Oversight
Governance for construction lending is structured to ensure accountability, transparency, and alignment with the bank’s risk
appetite. The Chief Credit Officer (CCO) retains ultimate responsibility for the approval and oversight of this policy. The
Construction Lending Committee (CLC), a subcommittee of the bank’s Credit Risk Committee, is tasked with reviewing and
approving all construction loan requests exceeding $10 million in exposure.
The CLC is composed of senior representatives from Credit Risk, Real Estate Lending, Legal, Compliance, and Finance. It
meets bi-weekly to review pending applications, monitor portfolio performance, and address emerging risks. Decisions of the
CLC are documented in minutes, which are retained for a minimum of seven years and made available to regulators upon
request.
Day-to-day oversight of construction lending activities is delegated to the Construction Risk Officer (CRO), who reports directly
to the CCO. The CRO is responsible for ensuring adherence to this policy, conducting periodic audits of construction loan
portfolios, and escalating material deviations or risks to the CLC. The CRO also maintains a watchlist of high-risk projects,
which is reviewed quarterly by the CLC.
Independent validation of compliance with this policy is performed annually by the bank’s Internal Audit function. Audit findings
are reported to the CCO and the Board’s Risk Committee, with corrective actions tracked to completion. Additionally, the bank’s
Compliance department conducts semi-annual reviews to ensure alignment with regulatory expectations, including those
outlined in the Interagency Guidelines for Real Estate Lending.
This governance structure is designed to foster a culture of risk awareness and accountability. All employees involved in
construction lending are required to complete annual training on this policy, with completion records maintained by Human
Resources. Failure to complete training may result in restrictions on an employee’s authority to participate in construction
lending activities.

4. 4. Underwriting Criteria
Underwriting for construction loans must adhere to stringent criteria to ensure the borrower’s financial capacity and the project’s
feasibility. The bank requires a minimum FICO score of 700 for individual borrowers or a minimum credit rating of BBB- for
corporate borrowers. For project-specific underwriting, the borrower must demonstrate a track record of successfully completing
at least three similar projects within the past five years, with no material defaults or cost overruns exceeding 10% of the original
budget.
The Loan-to-Cost (LTC) ratio for construction loans shall not exceed 80% for commercial projects or 85% for residential
projects. For speculative developments, the LTC ratio is capped at 70%. The Loan-to-Value (LTV) ratio, based on the appraised
value of the completed project, must not exceed 65% for commercial properties or 75% for residential properties. These
thresholds are designed to provide a buffer against cost overruns and market downturns.
Borrowers are required to contribute a minimum of 20% of the total project cost as equity, which must be injected prior to the
first disbursement of loan funds. Equity contributions may include cash, land (valued at no more than 50% of its appraised
value), or other unencumbered assets acceptable to the bank. The bank will not recognize sweat equity or future profits as valid
forms of equity contribution.
A comprehensive feasibility study must be submitted as part of the loan application, prepared by an independent third-party
consultant approved by the bank. The study must include detailed market analysis, pro forma financial projections, and
sensitivity analysis for key variables such as construction costs, absorption rates, and interest rates. The bank reserves the
right to commission its own feasibility study at the borrower’s expense if deemed necessary.
All construction loans must be supported by a first-priority lien on the property being developed, as well as personal or
corporate guarantees from the borrower. Additional collateral, such as assignments of contracts or letters of credit, may be
required at the discretion of the underwriter. The bank will not proceed with any construction loan without a valid, enforceable
security interest in place.

5. 5. Quantitative Limits and Thresholds
This policy establishes quantitative limits to control the bank’s exposure to construction lending risks. The maximum exposure
for any single construction loan is $50 million, unless approved by the CLC and the CCO. Aggregate exposure to construction
lending shall not exceed 25% of the bank’s total loan portfolio at any time. Additionally, the bank’s exposure to any single
borrower or borrower group for construction purposes is limited to 15% of the bank’s Tier 1 capital.
For speculative construction projects, the bank imposes a sub-limit of $25 million per loan and 10% of the total loan portfolio.
Speculative projects are defined as those where less than 50% of the units or space are pre-sold or pre-leased at the time of
loan closing. Projects exceeding these thresholds require additional approvals, including a unanimous vote by the CLC and
written justification from the Relationship Manager.
The bank maintains a contingency reserve requirement of 10% of the total project cost for all construction loans. This reserve is
held in a separate escrow account and released only upon completion of the project or as approved by the Construction Risk
Officer. In the event of cost overruns, the borrower is required to inject additional equity to cover the shortfall before any reserve
funds are released.
Interest rate risk is managed through the use of fixed-rate loans or interest rate caps for variable-rate construction loans. The
maximum allowable interest rate for construction loans is the bank’s prime rate plus 200 basis points. For loans with variable
rates, the bank requires a minimum debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) of 1.25x, calculated using a stressed interest rate of
prime + 300 basis points.
The bank also imposes limits on the duration of construction loans. The maximum term for a construction loan is 36 months,
with an option to extend for an additional 12 months subject to CLC approval. Loans that exceed 24 months in duration require
quarterly progress inspections by an independent third-party engineer, at the borrower’s expense. Failure to meet construction
milestones may result in the suspension of disbursements or acceleration of the loan.

6. 6. Approval Authorities and Escalation Paths
Approval authorities for construction loans are tiered based on the loan amount, risk profile, and complexity of the project.
Relationship Managers may approve construction loans up to $5 million, provided the loan meets all underwriting criteria and
the borrower has an existing relationship with the bank. Loans between $5 million and $10 million require approval from the
Regional Credit Officer (RCO) in addition to the Relationship Manager.
Loans exceeding $10 million must be approved by the Construction Lending Committee (CLC). The CLC’s approval is also
required for any loan that involves speculative development, a borrower with a credit rating below BBB-, or a project located in a
market where the bank has limited experience. The CLC’s decision is final, unless overridden by the Chief Credit Officer (CCO)
in exceptional circumstances.
Escalation paths are clearly defined to ensure timely resolution of issues. Any deviations from underwriting criteria, such as LTC
or LTV ratios exceeding policy limits, must be escalated to the RCO for review. The RCO has the authority to approve
exceptions up to 5% above the policy limits, provided the deviation is justified by compensating factors such as strong borrower
financials or pre-leasing commitments.
Material exceptions, defined as deviations exceeding 5% of policy limits or involving high-risk features such as speculative
development in an untried market, must be escalated to the CLC. The CLC will review the exception request, along with any
mitigating factors, and provide a written decision within 10 business days. All exception requests and decisions are documented
in the bank’s exception tracking system and reported to the CCO on a quarterly basis.
In cases where a construction loan exhibits signs of distress, such as cost overruns exceeding 10% of the budget or delays in
construction milestones, the Relationship Manager must immediately escalate the matter to the Construction Risk Officer
(CRO). The CRO will assess the situation and determine whether to place the loan on the watchlist, require additional collateral,
or take other risk mitigation actions. The CRO’s findings and recommendations are presented to the CLC for further action.

7. 7. Monitoring and Controls
Ongoing monitoring of construction loans is critical to identifying and addressing risks in a timely manner. The bank requires
monthly progress reports from the borrower, which must include updated construction budgets, disbursement requests, and
milestone achievements. These reports are reviewed by the Relationship Manager and forwarded to the Construction Risk
Officer (CRO) for validation.
In addition to borrower-provided reports, the bank conducts independent site inspections at least quarterly for all active
construction loans. Inspections are performed by third-party engineers approved by the bank and focus on verifying the physical
progress of the project, the quality of construction, and compliance with building codes and permits. Inspection reports are
submitted to the CRO and retained in the loan file.
The bank employs a series of early warning indicators to proactively identify potential issues. These include: (1) disbursement
requests exceeding 110% of the approved budget for any line item; (2) delays in achieving construction milestones by more
than 30 days; (3) a decline in the borrower’s credit rating or financial condition; or (4) adverse market conditions, such as a 10%
or greater decline in local real estate prices. Triggering any of these indicators requires immediate escalation to the CRO.
Controls are also in place to manage disbursements. Loan funds are disbursed in accordance with a pre-approved draw
schedule, which is tied to the achievement of specific construction milestones. Each disbursement request must be
accompanied by lien waivers from contractors and suppliers, as well as evidence of payment for prior disbursements. The bank
will not release funds for any milestone until all prior milestones have been completed and documented to the bank’s
satisfaction.
The CRO conducts a comprehensive portfolio review on a quarterly basis, which includes an assessment of each construction
loan’s performance against its approved budget, timeline, and financial projections. Loans identified as high-risk are subject to
enhanced monitoring, including more frequent inspections and reporting. The results of the portfolio review are presented to the
CLC and documented in a report to the CCO.

8. 8. Exception Handling
Exceptions to this policy are permitted only under limited circumstances and require formal approval. An exception is defined as
any deviation from the underwriting criteria, quantitative limits, or other requirements outlined in this document. All exceptions
must be documented in writing, justified by compensating factors, and approved by the appropriate authority as defined in
Section 6.
Compensating factors that may justify an exception include, but are not limited to: (1) a borrower with a long-standing
relationship with the bank and a proven track record of successful project completion; (2) pre-leasing or pre-sales commitments
that exceed 70% of the project’s capacity; (3) a project located in a high-demand market with limited supply; or (4) additional
collateral or guarantees provided by the borrower. The presence of compensating factors does not guarantee approval of an
exception request.
The exception request process begins with the Relationship Manager, who must submit a formal request to the RCO or CLC,
depending on the nature and size of the exception. The request must include a detailed explanation of the deviation, the
compensating factors, and the rationale for approval. The RCO or CLC will review the request, along with any supporting
documentation, and provide a written decision.
Approved exceptions are subject to enhanced monitoring and controls. For example, a loan approved with an LTC ratio
exceeding 80% may require monthly inspections instead of quarterly, or additional equity contributions from the borrower. The
terms of the exception, including any additional controls, are documented in the loan approval memo and monitored by the
CRO.
Exceptions that are denied or withdrawn must be documented, along with the reasons for the decision. The bank maintains a
log of all exception requests, including those that are approved, denied, or withdrawn, which is reviewed by Internal Audit as
part of its annual validation process. This log is also reported to the CCO and the Board’s Risk Committee on a semi-annual
basis.

9. 9. Reporting and Documentation
Reporting is a critical component of the bank’s construction lending program, ensuring transparency and accountability. The
Relationship Manager is responsible for preparing a monthly Construction Loan Portfolio Report, which includes a summary of
all active construction loans, their current status, disbursement activity, and any exceptions or issues. This report is submitted to

performance, including trends in delinquencies, cost overruns, and market conditions. This report also highlights any loans on

and distributed to the CCO, the Chief Risk Officer, and the Board’s Risk Committee.
Documentation requirements are stringent to ensure a complete audit trail for each construction loan. The loan file must
include, at a minimum: (1) the loan application and all supporting documentation, such as feasibility studies and appraisals; (2)
the underwriting memo, including the analysis of the borrower’s financial condition and the project’s viability; (3) the loan
approval memo, signed by the appropriate authority; (4) the draw schedule and all disbursement requests, along with
supporting documentation; and (5) all inspection reports, progress updates, and correspondence with the borrower.
The bank retains all construction loan documentation for a minimum of seven years after the loan is repaid or charged off.

personnel. Original hard copies of critical documents, such as signed loan agreements and security instruments, are retained in
a fireproof vault at the bank’s headquarters.

filings. This includes information on loan concentrations, delinquencies, and exceptions. The Compliance department is
responsible for ensuring that all regulatory reporting requirements are met and that the data submitted is accurate and
complete.

1. 1. Purpose and Applicability
This document, titled 'Clause 3.2: Escalation Rules,' is a synthetic demonstration policy derived from the parent framework

purposes only. While the thresholds, roles, and processes described herein are realistic and internally consistent, they do not
reflect the actual credit policies of any real financial institution. Users of this document must treat it as illustrative content and

This clause is effective immediately upon issuance and remains in force until superseded by a revised version or explicitly

2. 2. Scope of Escalation Requirements
The escalation requirements outlined in this clause apply to all credit exposures, including but not limited to loans, letters of
credit, guarantees, derivatives, and trade finance facilities. Escalation is mandatory for transactions that exceed the delegated
authority limits of the originating business unit or relationship manager, as well as for those that trigger risk-based thresholds
such as high probability of default (PD), loss given default (LGD), or exposure at default (EAD).
Quantitative thresholds for escalation are defined as follows: any single transaction exceeding USD 10 million in exposure must
be escalated to the next level of authority. For transactions between USD 5 million and USD 10 million, escalation is required if
the counterparty’s internal risk rating is below investment grade (i.e., BB+ or lower). Additionally, any transaction involving a
new counterparty in a high-risk jurisdiction, as defined by the bank’s Anti-Money Laundering (AML) policy, must be escalated
regardless of size.
Qualitative triggers for escalation include transactions involving complex structures, such as multi-jurisdictional collateral
arrangements or non-standard covenants. Escalation is also required for transactions where the borrower’s financial metrics
(e.g., leverage ratios, interest coverage) fall outside the bank’s standard underwriting tolerances by more than 20%.
Furthermore, any request for a waiver of standard credit terms, such as maturity extensions or covenant relief, must be
escalated to the appropriate authority level.
The scope of this policy extends to post-approval monitoring activities. For example, if a borrower’s credit quality deteriorates
such that its risk rating drops by two or more notches within a 12-month period, the relationship manager must escalate the
case to the Portfolio Risk Manager for review. Similarly, any breach of financial or non-financial covenants that is not cured
within the stipulated grace period must be escalated to the Credit Risk Committee (CRC).
Exclusions from this policy are limited to transactions that fall below the USD 1 million threshold and are classified as low-risk
under the bank’s internal risk assessment framework. However, even for such transactions, the relationship manager retains
the discretion to escalate if they deem it necessary based on qualitative factors or market conditions. The CCO may also direct
ad-hoc escalations for specific portfolios or counterparties as part of targeted risk reviews.

3. 3. Governance and Authority Framework
The governance framework for credit escalations is structured hierarchically to ensure that decisions are made at the
appropriate level of seniority and expertise. At the base of the hierarchy, Relationship Managers (RMs) are empowered to
approve transactions up to USD 1 million, provided they comply with all standard underwriting criteria and do not involve
high-risk counterparties or jurisdictions. RMs must document their rationale for approval in the bank’s credit management
system (CMS) and retain evidence of compliance with policy requirements.
The next level of authority resides with the Business Unit Credit Officers (BUCOs), who can approve transactions up to USD 5
million. BUCOs are also responsible for reviewing and endorsing or rejecting escalations from RMs for transactions that exceed
the RM’s delegated authority but fall within the BUCO’s limit. BUCOs must conduct an independent assessment of the credit
risk, including a review of the borrower’s financial statements, industry analysis, and collateral valuation, where applicable.
For transactions exceeding USD 5 million but not exceeding USD 25 million, escalation to the Regional Credit Officer (RCO) is
required. The RCO’s approval is also mandatory for any transaction involving a counterparty rated below BB- or domiciled in a
jurisdiction subject to sanctions or heightened AML scrutiny. The RCO must convene a credit review committee (CRC) for
transactions in this range that involve complex structures or significant policy exceptions.
Transactions exceeding USD 25 million, or those involving policy exceptions that cannot be resolved at the RCO level, must be
escalated to the Chief Credit Officer (CCO). The CCO’s approval is final for all credit decisions, except in cases where the
transaction exceeds USD 100 million or involves a new product type not previously approved by the bank. In such instances,
the CCO must seek ratification from the bank’s Board of Directors or its designated Risk Committee.
The authority framework is supported by a system of checks and balances, including independent risk reviews by the bank’s
Risk Management Division (RMD) and compliance attestations by the Legal and Compliance teams. All escalations must be
documented in the CMS, with clear audit trails showing the rationale for decisions, the evidence reviewed, and the identities of
the approving authorities. The Internal Audit function conducts periodic reviews of escalation compliance as part of its broader
mandate to assess the effectiveness of the bank’s credit risk controls.

4. 4. Underwriting Criteria and Risk Assessment
Underwriting criteria serve as the foundation for determining whether a transaction requires escalation under this policy. The
bank’s standard underwriting framework evaluates counterparties based on five core risk dimensions: financial strength,
industry risk, management quality, collateral coverage, and structural subordination. Each dimension is scored on a scale of 1
to 5, with 1 representing the lowest risk and 5 the highest. A composite risk score is calculated as the weighted average of
these dimensions, with financial strength and industry risk each accounting for 30% of the total score, and the remaining
dimensions accounting for 10% each.
Transactions with a composite risk score of 3.0 or higher must be escalated to the BUCO, regardless of size. Similarly, any
transaction where a single risk dimension scores a 5 must be escalated to the RCO, as this indicates a critical weakness that
could materially impact the bank’s risk exposure. For example, a counterparty with a financial strength score of 5 (e.g., negative
equity or persistent cash flow deficits) would trigger an automatic escalation, even if the other dimensions are scored more
favorably.
In addition to the composite risk score, the bank employs a series of quantitative thresholds to identify transactions requiring
escalation. These include debt service coverage ratios (DSCR) below 1.25x, leverage ratios (total debt to EBITDA) above 4.0x,
and current ratios below 1.0x. Transactions breaching any of these thresholds must be escalated to the next level of authority,
with the escalation path determined by the severity and number of breaches. For instance, a transaction breaching two or more
thresholds would require RCO approval, while a single breach might be addressed at the BUCO level.
Qualitative underwriting criteria also play a critical role in determining escalation requirements. These include assessments of
the borrower’s business model sustainability, competitive positioning, and exposure to environmental, social, and governance
(ESG) risks. For example, a borrower operating in a sector facing significant regulatory disruption (e.g., fossil fuel extraction)
may require escalation to the RCO or CCO, even if its financial metrics are within standard thresholds. Similarly, transactions
involving related-party exposures or complex intercompany guarantees must be escalated to ensure that conflicts of interest are
appropriately managed.
The underwriting criteria are reviewed and updated annually by the Credit Policy Committee (CPC) to reflect changes in market
conditions, regulatory requirements, and the bank’s risk appetite. Any material changes to the criteria must be approved by the
CCO and communicated to all relevant stakeholders through the bank’s policy management system. Relationship Managers
are required to complete annual training on the underwriting framework and pass a competency assessment to retain their
delegated authority.

5. 5. Quantitative Limits and Thresholds
Quantitative limits are a cornerstone of the bank’s credit escalation framework, providing objective triggers for when
transactions must be reviewed by higher authorities. The bank employs a tiered system of limits, which are applied at both the
individual transaction and aggregate exposure levels. At the transaction level, the primary limits are as follows: USD 1 million for
Relationship Managers, USD 5 million for Business Unit Credit Officers, USD 25 million for Regional Credit Officers, and USD

100 million for the Chief Credit Officer. Transactions exceeding these limits must be escalated to the next authority level, as
outlined in Section 3.
Aggregate exposure limits are applied to counterparties, industries, and geographic regions to prevent excessive concentration
risk. For example, the bank’s single counterparty exposure limit is set at 10% of its Tier 1 capital, while the aggregate exposure
to any single industry sector cannot exceed 20% of Tier 1 capital. Exposures approaching or exceeding 80% of these limits
must be escalated to the CCO for review, and any breaches must be reported to the Board of Directors within 48 hours. The
bank’s Risk Management Division (RMD) monitors aggregate exposures in real-time and generates automated alerts when
thresholds are approached.
In addition to exposure limits, the bank enforces risk-based thresholds for specific credit metrics. For corporate borrowers,
these include a maximum leverage ratio of 4.5x, a minimum interest coverage ratio of 2.0x, and a minimum current ratio of 1.2x.
For retail portfolios, thresholds include a maximum delinquency rate of 3% and a minimum FICO score of 650 for new
originations. Transactions or portfolios breaching these thresholds must be escalated according to the severity of the breach,
with more significant deviations requiring higher levels of approval.
The bank also applies concentration limits to specific asset classes and products. For example, exposures to commercial real
estate (CRE) cannot exceed 300% of the bank’s total risk-weighted assets, and within the CRE portfolio, no more than 15% of
the total CRE exposure can be concentrated in a single geographic market. Similarly, the bank limits its exposure to
speculative-grade (below BB-) counterparties to 5% of Tier 1 capital. Any transaction that would cause the bank to exceed
these concentration limits must be escalated to the CCO for exception approval.
Quantitative limits and thresholds are reviewed quarterly by the CPC, which may adjust them based on changes in the bank’s
risk appetite, capital position, or macroeconomic outlook. The CCO has the authority to impose temporary, more restrictive
limits in response to emerging risks or market dislocations. All changes to quantitative limits must be documented in the bank’s
policy management system and communicated to relevant stakeholders within 5 business days of approval.

6. 6. Approval Workflows and Delegated Authority
Approval workflows under this policy are designed to ensure that credit decisions are made efficiently while maintaining robust
risk controls. The workflows are automated through the bank’s Credit Management System (CMS), which routes transactions to
the appropriate authority based on predefined rules, including transaction size, counterparty risk rating, and product type. The
CMS also flags transactions that require escalation due to policy exceptions, threshold breaches, or qualitative risk factors,
ensuring that no high-risk transaction is approved without the necessary oversight.
For transactions within a Relationship Manager’s (RM) delegated authority, the workflow requires the RM to complete a credit
application in the CMS, which includes a detailed assessment of the borrower’s creditworthiness, proposed terms, and
supporting documentation (e.g., financial statements, collateral valuations). The CMS automatically validates the application
against the bank’s underwriting criteria and quantitative thresholds. If the transaction complies with all requirements, the RM
may approve it directly. However, if the CMS identifies any issues, the transaction is automatically escalated to the BUCO for
review.
Transactions requiring BUCO approval follow a similar process, with the BUCO conducting an independent review of the RM’s
assessment. The BUCO must document their rationale for approval or rejection in the CMS, including any mitigating factors or
additional controls they deem necessary. If the BUCO approves the transaction, it is automatically routed to the RCO for
information purposes, though RCO approval is not required unless the transaction exceeds the BUCO’s delegated authority.
The CMS maintains a log of all approvals, including timestamps and the identities of the approving authorities, to ensure full
auditability.
For transactions requiring RCO or CCO approval, the workflow includes additional steps to ensure thorough due diligence. The
RCO or CCO must convene a credit review committee (CRC), which includes representatives from Risk Management, Legal,
Compliance, and the relevant business unit. The CRC reviews the transaction in detail, including a presentation by the RM and
a challenge session led by the RCO or CCO. The CRC’s recommendation is documented in the CMS, and the final decision is
recorded with the approving authority’s digital signature. Transactions requiring Board approval follow a similar process, with
the CCO presenting the case to the Board’s Risk Committee for ratification.
Delegated authority may be temporarily suspended or revised by the CCO in cases of repeated policy breaches, significant
credit losses, or changes in the risk profile of a business unit or region. The CCO must notify affected employees in writing and
update the CMS to reflect the changes. Delegated authority is also subject to annual recertification, which requires employees
to demonstrate ongoing competence in credit risk management through training and assessments. Failure to complete
recertification results in the automatic revocation of delegated authority until the requirements are met.

8. 8. Exception Handling and Waivers
Exceptions to the bank’s standard credit policies, including underwriting criteria, quantitative thresholds, or approval workflows,
are permitted only under strictly controlled circumstances. This section outlines the process for requesting, reviewing, and
approving exceptions, as well as the controls in place to ensure that such exceptions do not expose the bank to unacceptable
risks. All exceptions must be justified by compelling business or strategic rationale and must be supported by robust risk
mitigants.
The process for requesting an exception begins with the Relationship Manager (RM), who must submit a formal exception
request through the Credit Management System (CMS). The request must include a detailed business case, an assessment of
the incremental risk introduced by the exception, and a description of the mitigating factors or controls that will be implemented
to offset the risk. The RM must also provide evidence that the borrower or transaction has been subjected to enhanced due
diligence, such as additional financial analysis, third-party risk assessments, or legal opinions.
Exception requests are reviewed by the Business Unit Credit Officer (BUCO), who assesses the merits of the case and the
adequacy of the proposed mitigants. The BUCO may approve exceptions for transactions within their delegated authority,
provided that the incremental risk is deemed acceptable and the mitigants are sufficient. However, exceptions that involve
policy breaches, such as waivers of standard covenants or underwriting criteria, must be escalated to the Regional Credit
Officer (RCO) for approval. The RCO may consult with the bank’s Risk Management Division (RMD) or Legal team to assess
the implications of the exception.
Exceptions that cannot be resolved at the RCO level, or those involving transactions exceeding USD 25 million, must be
escalated to the Chief Credit Officer (CCO). The CCO has the authority to approve exceptions that are consistent with the
bank’s risk appetite and strategic objectives. However, exceptions that involve material deviations from the bank’s credit
policies, such as transactions with counterparties rated below B- or exposures exceeding 15% of Tier 1 capital, require the
approval of the Board’s Risk Committee. The CCO must present such cases to the committee, including a detailed risk
assessment and a recommendation for approval or rejection.
All approved exceptions are documented in the CMS, with clear records of the rationale, the mitigating factors, and the identities
of the approving authorities. The bank’s Internal Audit function conducts periodic reviews of exception handling to ensure
compliance with this policy and to assess the effectiveness of the controls in place. Exceptions are also subject to post-approval
monitoring, with the RM required to provide quarterly updates on the performance of the transaction and the continued validity
of the mitigating factors. If the risk profile of the transaction deteriorates, the RM must escalate the case for reassessment,
which may result in the withdrawal of the exception or the imposition of additional controls.

1. 1. Purpose and Objectives
This synthetic credit policy document, designated as Clause A.1 under the parent policy REG-Basel-IV, establishes the

regulatory capital requirements. By defining clear methodologies for RWA calculation, this policy aims to enhance the accuracy
of capital adequacy reporting and support prudent risk-taking.
The objectives of this policy include: (i) providing a structured approach to assigning risk weights to credit exposures; (ii)
ensuring consistency in the application of RWA treatments across all business units; (iii) facilitating transparency in the bank’s
capital allocation processes; and (iv) enabling effective monitoring of credit risk concentrations. This policy is designed to be
internally consistent with the bank’s broader risk management framework, including credit underwriting, portfolio monitoring,
and regulatory reporting.

financial institution. It is intended solely for illustrative purposes to demonstrate how a bank might structure its RWA treatment
policy under Basel IV. All thresholds, roles, and processes described herein are fictional and should not be interpreted as
operational guidelines.
The policy is grounded in the principle that RWA calculations must reflect the true economic risk of credit exposures. To achieve
this, the bank adopts a combination of the Standardized Approach and the Internal Ratings-Based (IRB) Approach, as
permitted under Basel IV. The choice of approach depends on the nature of the exposure, the availability of historical data, and
the sophistication of the bank’s risk management systems. The policy ensures that all approaches are applied consistently and
are subject to regular validation.
Compliance with this policy is mandatory for all business units involved in credit risk management, including lending, treasury,
and risk control functions. Failure to adhere to the RWA treatment guidelines may result in misalignment with regulatory capital
requirements, potentially leading to reputational, financial, or regulatory risks. The policy is reviewed annually to ensure its
continued relevance and alignment with evolving regulatory expectations.

4. 4. Underwriting Criteria and Risk Classification
The underwriting criteria for RWA treatment are aligned with the bank’s broader credit risk policies and are designed to ensure
that all exposures are classified accurately based on their risk characteristics. The policy mandates that all new credit
exposures undergo a comprehensive risk assessment before approval, which includes an evaluation of the borrower’s
creditworthiness, the nature of the exposure, and the availability of collateral or guarantees.
For corporate exposures, the bank uses a combination of external credit ratings and internal risk assessments to determine the
appropriate risk weight. Exposures to borrowers with an investment-grade rating (BBB- or higher) are assigned a risk weight of
50%, while those with a speculative-grade rating (BB+ or lower) are assigned a risk weight of 100% or higher, depending on the
specific rating. For unrated exposures, the bank applies its internal risk rating methodology, which categorizes borrowers into
risk buckets ranging from 1 (lowest risk) to 10 (highest risk), with corresponding risk weights of 20% to 150%.
Retail exposures, such as mortgages and personal loans, are subject to a separate risk classification framework. The bank
uses a scorecard-based approach to assess the creditworthiness of retail borrowers, with risk weights assigned based on the
probability of default (PD) and loss given default (LGD) estimates. For example, retail exposures with a PD of less than 1% are
assigned a risk weight of 35%, while those with a PD of 5% or higher are assigned a risk weight of 100%.
The policy also addresses the treatment of collateral and guarantees in RWA calculations. Collateralized exposures are eligible
for a reduction in risk weight, provided that the collateral meets the bank’s eligibility criteria and is legally enforceable. The
maximum reduction in risk weight is 50%, subject to a floor of 20%. Guarantees from eligible third parties, such as sovereigns
or highly rated financial institutions, may also result in a reduction in risk weight, depending on the credit quality of the
guarantor.

5. 5. Quantitative Limits and Thresholds
This policy establishes quantitative limits and thresholds to ensure that the bank’s RWA calculations remain within acceptable
risk parameters. The most critical threshold is the minimum capital requirement, which is set at 8% of total RWA, in line with
Basel IV. The bank’s internal target is to maintain a Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital ratio of at least 10%, providing a
buffer above the regulatory minimum to account for potential stress scenarios.
The policy also sets concentration limits for specific sectors, geographies, and borrower types to prevent excessive risk
exposure. For example, the bank limits its exposure to any single industry sector to 20% of total RWA. Similarly, exposures to
borrowers in high-risk jurisdictions, as defined by the bank’s country risk classification, are capped at 15% of total RWA. These
limits are monitored on a quarterly basis, and any breaches must be reported to the RMC within five business days.
In addition to concentration limits, the policy specifies thresholds for the use of internal models in RWA calculations. Under the
IRB Approach, the bank is permitted to use internal estimates of PD, LGD, and exposure at default (EAD) for certain asset
classes, provided that the models meet the regulatory criteria for validation and approval. The policy mandates that internal
models must be backtested annually, with a maximum tolerance of 5% deviation between estimated and actual outcomes.
Models that fail to meet this threshold are subject to remediation or replacement.
The bank also imposes limits on the use of credit risk mitigation techniques, such as collateral and guarantees. For example,
the policy states that the total reduction in RWA attributable to collateral and guarantees cannot exceed 30% of the bank’s total
RWA. This limit is designed to prevent over-reliance on risk mitigation techniques, which may not be effective in all scenarios.

reduction.

6. 6. Approval Authorities and Escalation Paths
The approval authorities for RWA treatment are structured to ensure that decisions are made at the appropriate level of
seniority, based on the complexity and risk of the exposure. The policy defines three tiers of approval authority: (i) Business Unit
Heads, (ii) Regional Risk Committees, and (iii) the Group Risk Management Committee (RMC). Each tier has specific
delegated authorities and escalation paths to ensure that higher-risk decisions receive the necessary oversight.
Business Unit Heads are authorized to approve RWA treatments for exposures up to USD 10 million, provided that the
exposure complies with the bank’s standard underwriting criteria and risk classification frameworks. Approvals must be
documented in the bank’s credit approval system, with supporting evidence including the borrower’s credit rating, financial
statements, and collateral valuation (where applicable). Business Unit Heads are also responsible for ensuring that all approved
exposures are monitored in accordance with the policy’s monitoring requirements.
Regional Risk Committees (RRCs) are responsible for approving RWA treatments for exposures between USD 10 million and
USD 50 million, as well as any exposures that do not meet the standard underwriting criteria. The RRCs are composed of
senior representatives from the Credit Risk Department, Business Units, and Legal and Compliance functions. Approvals by the
RRCs must be supported by a detailed credit memo, which includes an analysis of the exposure’s risk characteristics, the
proposed RWA treatment, and any mitigating factors.
The Group RMC is the final approval authority for all exposures exceeding USD 50 million, as well as any exposures that
involve novel or complex structures, such as synthetic securitizations or credit derivatives. The RMC reviews these exposures
on a case-by-case basis, with input from the bank’s Legal, Compliance, and Finance departments. The RMC’s decision is
documented in a resolution, which is retained in the bank’s central repository for audit purposes.
Escalation paths are clearly defined to ensure that any disputes or exceptions to the policy are resolved promptly. For example,
if a Business Unit Head disagrees with the RWA treatment proposed by the Credit Risk Department, the matter must be
escalated to the relevant RRC for resolution. Similarly, if an RRC is unable to reach a consensus on a high-risk exposure, the
matter is escalated to the Group RMC. This synthetic escalation framework is designed to demonstrate how a bank might
ensure consistent and prudent decision-making in its RWA treatment processes.

models. This validation is performed by an independent team within the CRD and includes a comprehensive assessment of the

8. 8. Exceptions and Waivers
The bank recognizes that there may be circumstances where strict adherence to the RWA treatment policy is not feasible or

of strategic importance to the bank. For example, an exception may be requested for a high-profile corporate client where the
bank has a long-standing relationship and a strong understanding of the client’s risk profile. Exceptions must be supported by a
detailed business case, which includes an analysis of the exposure’s risk characteristics, the proposed RWA treatment, and the
rationale for deviating from the policy.
Waivers may be granted for exposures where the application of the standard RWA treatment would result in an outcome that is
not aligned with the true economic risk of the exposure. For example, a waiver may be requested for a collateralized exposure
where the collateral’s value significantly exceeds the exposure amount, making the standard risk weight overly conservative.
Waivers must be supported by a robust analysis, including an independent valuation of the collateral and a comparison of the
proposed RWA treatment against alternative approaches.
All exceptions and waivers must be approved by the appropriate authority, based on the size and risk of the exposure.
Exceptions for exposures up to USD 10 million may be approved by the Business Unit Head, while exceptions for exposures
between USD 10 million and USD 50 million require approval from the relevant Regional Risk Committee (RRC). Exceptions for
exposures exceeding USD 50 million, or those involving novel or complex structures, must be approved by the Group Risk
Management Committee (RMC).
The policy requires that all exceptions and waivers be documented in the bank’s central repository, with a clear audit trail of the
approval process. Exceptions and waivers are subject to periodic review, typically on an annual basis, to ensure that they
remain justified and appropriate. This synthetic section on exceptions and waivers illustrates how a bank might balance
flexibility with prudence in its RWA treatment processes, while maintaining strong governance and documentation standards.

adhere to its requirements. The RMC meets quarterly to review the effectiveness of the Policy, assess compliance with capital
floor requirements, and address any emerging risks or issues. Minutes of these meetings, including action items and decisions,
are documented and made available to the Board and relevant regulators upon request.
The RMD, under the leadership of the CRO, is tasked with the operational implementation of the Policy. This includes
developing procedures, tools, and methodologies for calculating and monitoring capital floors, as well as providing training and
guidance to business units. The RMD is also responsible for conducting independent reviews and audits to verify compliance
with the Policy.
Business unit heads are accountable for ensuring that their respective areas comply with the Policy. They must designate a
Capital Floor Coordinator within their unit to serve as the primary point of contact for the RMD. Coordinators are responsible for
providing accurate and timely data, addressing any non-compliance issues, and escalating material risks or breaches to the
RMC.
The Internal Audit Department (IAD) conducts an annual audit of the Policy’s effectiveness and the Bank’s compliance with its
requirements. The audit includes a review of the capital floor calculations, the accuracy of RWAs, and the adequacy of controls
and escalation procedures. Findings and recommendations from the audit are presented to the RMC and the Board for action.

4. 4. Underwriting Criteria
The underwriting criteria outlined in this section are designed to ensure that all credit exposures subject to the Capital Floors
Policy are originated and managed in a manner consistent with the Bank’s risk appetite and regulatory requirements. These
criteria apply to all new and renewed exposures, including loans, derivatives, and other credit facilities.
For credit exposures assessed under the IRB approach, the Bank must ensure that the estimated Probability of Default (PD),
Loss Given Default (LGD), and Exposure at Default (EAD) parameters are conservative and supported by robust historical data
and forward-looking analysis. The PD, LGD, and EAD estimates must be validated annually by an independent party, such as
the Model Validation Team (MVT), to ensure their accuracy and reliability.
The Bank’s underwriting process must incorporate a capital floor assessment for all material exposures. This assessment
involves comparing the RWAs calculated under the IRB approach with those calculated under the standardized approach. If the
IRB RWAs are less than 72.5% of the standardized RWAs, the difference must be justified and documented. Justifications must
be based on objective evidence, such as the quality of the underlying data, the robustness of the model, or the specific risk
characteristics of the exposure.
For exposures where the capital floor is breached, the underwriting process must include an escalation to the RMC for
approval. The escalation must include a detailed analysis of the reasons for the breach, the potential risks, and the proposed
mitigation measures. The RMC may approve the exposure if it is satisfied that the risks are adequately managed and that the
breach does not pose a material threat to the Bank’s capital adequacy.
The underwriting criteria also require that all credit exposures be subject to ongoing monitoring and review. This includes
regular updates to the PD, LGD, and EAD parameters, as well as periodic reassessments of the capital floor compliance. Any
material changes in the risk profile of an exposure must be reported to the RMD and, if necessary, escalated to the RMC.

5. 5. Quantitative Limits
The Capital Floors Policy establishes quantitative limits to ensure that the Bank’s capital adequacy ratio remains above the
minimum regulatory requirements. The primary limit is the capital floor, which is set at 72.5% of the RWAs calculated using the
standardized approach. This means that the RWAs calculated under the Bank’s internal models must not be less than 72.5% of
the RWAs calculated under the standardized approach for the same exposures.
In addition to the capital floor, the Policy introduces a series of internal triggers and thresholds to monitor and manage capital
adequacy. The first trigger is activated when the Bank’s Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital ratio falls below 10.5%. At this
point, the RMD must conduct a detailed review of the Bank’s capital position and submit a report to the RMC within 10 business
days, outlining the causes of the decline and the proposed corrective actions.
A second trigger is activated when the CET1 capital ratio falls below 9.5%. In this case, the RMC must convene an emergency
meeting within 5 business days to assess the situation and develop a capital restoration plan. The plan must include specific
measures to improve the capital ratio, such as reducing risk-weighted assets, raising additional capital, or divesting non-core
assets. The plan must be approved by the Board and submitted to the relevant regulators within 15 business days.
The Policy also establishes a maximum leverage ratio of 5%, calculated as the ratio of the Bank’s Tier 1 capital to its total
exposure measure. The total exposure measure includes both on-balance sheet and off-balance sheet exposures. If the
leverage ratio exceeds 5%, the Bank must immediately notify the RMC and implement measures to reduce the ratio to within
the limit.
For trading book exposures, the Policy sets a limit on the Value-at-Risk (VaR) capital charge. The VaR capital charge must not
exceed 3 times the average VaR capital charge over the previous 60 business days. If this limit is breached, the Bank must
conduct a review of its trading activities and risk management practices and report the findings to the RMC.

6. 6. Approvals
The approvals process under this Policy is designed to ensure that all material decisions related to capital floors are subject to
appropriate oversight and accountability. Approvals are required for the initial implementation of the Policy, any subsequent
amendments, and all exceptions or breaches of the Policy’s requirements.
Amendments to the Policy must be approved by the RMC and the Board. The process begins with a proposal from the RMD,
which is reviewed by the RMC. If the RMC approves the proposal, it is submitted to the Board for final approval. Amendments
are typically reviewed annually, but ad-hoc reviews may be conducted if there are significant changes in regulatory
requirements or the Bank’s risk profile.
Exceptions to the Policy’s requirements, such as exclusions from the scope or justifications for capital floor breaches, must be
approved by the RMC. Requests for exceptions must be submitted by the relevant business unit to the RMD, which conducts an
initial review and provides a recommendation to the RMC. The RMC considers the request at its next scheduled meeting or, if
urgent, at an ad-hoc meeting. Approvals for exceptions are valid for a maximum of 12 months, after which they must be
reviewed and reapproved.
Breaches of the capital floor or other quantitative limits must be reported to the RMC within 24 hours of identification. The RMC
must then determine whether the breach is material and, if so, escalate it to the Board. Material breaches are those that exceed
5% of the Bank’s total RWAs or result in a CET1 capital ratio below 9.5%. The RMC or Board, as applicable, must approve a
remediation plan to address the breach within 10 business days.
The Policy also requires approvals for the introduction of new internal models or significant changes to existing models. These
must be approved by the MVT, the RMC, and, in some cases, the relevant regulators. The approval process includes a
thorough validation of the model’s assumptions, methodologies, and performance, as well as an assessment of its impact on
the Bank’s capital floors.

7. 7. Monitoring
The monitoring framework under this Policy is designed to ensure continuous compliance with capital floor requirements and to
provide early warning of potential breaches or risks. Monitoring is conducted at multiple levels, including business units, the
RMD, and the RMC, to ensure comprehensive coverage and timely escalation.
Business units are responsible for monitoring their own exposures and capital floor compliance on a daily basis. This includes
tracking RWAs calculated under both internal models and the standardized approach, as well as monitoring the capital floor
ratio for each material exposure. Business units must report any breaches or potential breaches to the RMD within 24 hours of
identification.
The RMD conducts independent monitoring of the Bank’s overall capital floor compliance on a weekly basis. This includes
aggregating data from all business units, validating the accuracy of RWAs, and assessing the Bank’s compliance with the

72.5% capital floor requirement. The RMD also monitors the Bank’s CET1 capital ratio, leverage ratio, and other quantitative
limits established under the Policy. Any breaches or trends that could lead to breaches are reported to the RMC.
The RMC reviews the Bank’s capital floor compliance on a monthly basis. This review includes an assessment of the Bank’s
overall capital position, the effectiveness of the monitoring framework, and the status of any remediation plans for breaches or
exceptions. The RMC also reviews the results of the internal audits and independent validations conducted by the IAD and the
MVT.
In addition to regular monitoring, the Policy requires the conduct of stress tests and scenario analyses on a semi-annual basis.
These tests assess the impact of adverse economic conditions, market shocks, or operational failures on the Bank’s capital
floors and overall capital adequacy. The results of the stress tests are reported to the RMC and the Board and are used to
inform the Bank’s capital planning and risk management strategies.
The Bank’s monitoring framework is supported by a suite of automated tools and systems that provide real-time data on RWAs,
capital ratios, and other key metrics. These tools are subject to regular validation and testing to ensure their accuracy and
reliability. The RMD is responsible for maintaining and updating these tools as necessary.

8. 8. Exceptions
The Policy recognizes that there may be circumstances where strict adherence to the capital floor requirements is not feasible
or appropriate. In such cases, exceptions may be granted, provided that they are justified, documented, and approved through
the established governance framework. Exceptions are intended to be rare and are subject to strict controls and monitoring.
Exceptions may be requested for individual exposures, portfolios, or business units. Common reasons for exceptions include
the unavailability of reliable data for the standardized approach, the unique risk characteristics of an exposure that are not
captured by the internal models, or the temporary nature of a breach due to market conditions. However, exceptions cannot be
granted for systemic or persistent breaches of the capital floor.
Requests for exceptions must be submitted to the RMD using the standardized Exception Request Form. The form requires a
detailed justification for the exception, including the specific circumstances that warrant it, the potential risks, and the proposed
mitigation measures. The request must also include an assessment of the impact of the exception on the Bank’s capital
adequacy and a plan for monitoring and reviewing the exception.
The RMD reviews the request and provides a recommendation to the RMC. The RMC considers the request at its next
scheduled meeting or, if urgent, at an ad-hoc meeting. The RMC’s decision is based on the merits of the request, the potential
risks to the Bank, and the adequacy of the proposed mitigation measures. If approved, the exception is documented in the
Exception Register, which is maintained by the RMD and reviewed by the RMC on a quarterly basis.
Exceptions are valid for a maximum of 12 months, after which they must be reviewed and reapproved. The RMD is responsible
for monitoring the status of all exceptions and ensuring that they remain justified and appropriate. If the circumstances that
warranted the exception change, the RMD must reassess the exception and, if necessary, recommend its revocation to the
RMC.
All exceptions must be reported to the relevant regulators as part of the Bank’s regular regulatory reporting. The report must
include the number of exceptions, their justification, and the status of any remediation plans. The Bank must also be prepared
to provide additional information or explanations to the regulators upon request.

9. 9. Reporting
The reporting framework under this Policy is designed to provide timely, accurate, and comprehensive information on the
Bank’s capital floor compliance to senior management, the Board, and relevant regulators. Reporting is conducted at multiple
levels and frequencies to ensure that all stakeholders are informed and that issues are escalated promptly.
Business units are required to submit weekly reports to the RMD on their capital floor compliance. These reports must include
the RWAs calculated under both internal models and the standardized approach, the capital floor ratio for each material
exposure, and any breaches or potential breaches. The reports must also include an explanation of any significant changes in
the RWAs or capital floor ratios, as well as the status of any remediation plans for breaches.
The RMD consolidates the business unit reports and submits a monthly Capital Floor Compliance Report to the RMC. This
report provides an overview of the Bank’s overall capital floor compliance, including aggregate RWAs, capital floor ratios, and
the status of any breaches or exceptions. The report also includes an assessment of the effectiveness of the monitoring
framework and any emerging risks or trends.
The RMC reviews the monthly report and submits a quarterly Capital Floor Summary Report to the Board. This report provides
a high-level overview of the Bank’s capital floor compliance, including key metrics, trends, and any material breaches or
exceptions. The report also includes an assessment of the Bank’s overall capital adequacy and the effectiveness of the Policy’s
implementation.
In addition to internal reporting, the Bank is required to submit regular reports to the relevant regulators on its capital floor
compliance. These reports are typically submitted quarterly and include detailed information on the Bank’s RWAs, capital floor
ratios, and any breaches or exceptions. The reports must be accurate, complete, and submitted by the regulatory deadlines.
The Policy also requires ad-hoc reporting for material breaches or exceptions. These reports must be submitted to the RMC
and the relevant regulators within 24 hours of identification. Ad-hoc reports must include a detailed description of the breach or
exception, its causes, the potential risks, and the proposed remediation plan. The RMC and regulators may request additional
information or explanations as needed.

10. 10. Review
The review process under this Policy is designed to ensure that the Policy remains relevant, effective, and aligned with the
Bank’s strategic objectives and regulatory requirements. Reviews are conducted at regular intervals and in response to
significant changes in the Bank’s operating environment or risk profile.
The Policy is subject to an annual review, which is led by the RMD and overseen by the RMC. The review process includes an
assessment of the Policy’s effectiveness in achieving its objectives, as well as an evaluation of its alignment with the Basel IV
requirements and other relevant regulations. The review also considers feedback from business units, the IAD, and the MVT, as
well as any findings or recommendations from internal audits or independent validations.
As part of the annual review, the RMD conducts a comprehensive assessment of the Bank’s capital floor compliance over the
previous 12 months. This includes a review of the number and severity of breaches, the effectiveness of the monitoring and
reporting frameworks, and the adequacy of the remediation plans for any breaches or exceptions. The assessment also
considers the results of the stress tests and scenario analyses conducted during the year.
In addition to the annual review, the Policy may be reviewed ad-hoc in response to significant changes in the Bank’s risk profile,
regulatory requirements, or operating environment. Such changes may include the introduction of new products or services, the
acquisition or divestiture of business units, or the implementation of new regulatory standards. Ad-hoc reviews are conducted
by the RMD and submitted to the RMC for approval.
The results of the annual and ad-hoc reviews are documented in a Policy Review Report, which is submitted to the RMC and
the Board for approval. The report includes a summary of the review findings, any proposed amendments to the Policy, and a
plan for implementing the amendments. The RMC and Board must approve the report and any proposed amendments before
they are implemented.
The Policy Review Report is also submitted to the relevant regulators as part of the Bank’s regular regulatory reporting. The
report provides the regulators with assurance that the Policy remains effective and aligned with regulatory requirements. The
Bank must be prepared to provide additional information or explanations to the regulators upon request.

1. 1. Purpose and Applicability
This document, titled RAT-1.0 Credit Rating Standards, establishes the foundational framework for credit rating assignments
within the synthetic demonstration environment of the bank. It is designed to ensure consistency, transparency, and regulatory
compliance in the evaluation of creditworthiness for all counterparties, including corporate, commercial, and retail clients. The
standards outlined herein are aligned with the parent policy RAT-v1.0 and serve as a critical component of the bank’s risk
management infrastructure.
The primary purpose of RAT-1.0 is to define the methodologies, criteria, and governance structures required to assign, validate,
and monitor credit ratings. These ratings are integral to the bank’s decision-making processes, including loan approvals,
risk-based pricing, capital allocation, and portfolio monitoring. By adhering to these standards, the bank aims to mitigate credit
risk, enhance stakeholder confidence, and fulfill its fiduciary responsibilities.
This policy applies to all business units, risk management teams, and personnel involved in the credit assessment process. It is
mandatory for underwriters, credit analysts, relationship managers, and senior management to comply with the provisions of
this document. Third-party vendors or partners engaged in credit-related activities on behalf of the bank must also adhere to
these standards unless explicitly exempted by the Chief Risk Officer (CRO).
The synthetic nature of this document is emphasized to clarify that it is intended for demonstration, training, and internal testing
purposes only. While the thresholds, roles, and processes described are realistic and internally consistent, they do not reflect
actual bank operations or real-world data. Any use of this document for live transactions or external reporting must be explicitly
authorized by the bank’s compliance and legal departments.
The applicability of RAT-1.0 extends to all credit exposures, including but not limited to loans, bonds, derivatives, and trade
finance instruments. It covers both new credit applications and the periodic review of existing exposures. The standards are
designed to be scalable, accommodating the diverse needs of the bank’s global operations while maintaining uniformity in risk
assessment practices.
